bytes("x").pad_start(3, 'é')        // Error: invalid_value — the fill does not fit a single element
bytes("x").pad_start(3, "ab")       // Error: invalid_argument_type — fill is one element

members.name: pad_start_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `pad_start`.

members.name: partition
members.summary: Split at the first separator hit into exactly three pieces, `[before, sep, after]`.

doc.markdown:
A miss answers `[b, bytes(), bytes()]`. With no argument the separator is the whole first maximal run of blank
octets. Separators take the same menu as [`split`](kavun:type/bytes/split); the pieces are `bytes`.

doc.code: bytes("k=v=w").partition("=")       // => [bytes([107]), bytes([61]), bytes([118, 61, 119])]

members.name: prepend
members.summary: Add the arguments at the front as whole operands, in argument order; see [`append`](kavun:type/bytes/append).

members.name: prepend_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `prepend`.

members.name: push
members.summary: Add each argument at the back as exactly **one element**; a sequence argument raises, even at length 1, and so does a multi-octet rune.

doc.markdown:
`push`/`push_first` are the validating forms: **one element per argument** — a sequence argument raises even at
length 1, and a multi-octet rune raises too (it does not fit one element).

doc.code:
bytes("ab").push(98)                // => bytes([97, 98, 98]) — an in-range int is one octet
bytes("ab").push(b'\xff')           // => bytes([97, 98, 255])
bytes("ab").push('c')               // => bytes([97, 98, 99]) — ASCII rune = one octet
bytes("ab").push(256)               // Error: invalid_value: (push) an int reads as one octet and must be in [0, 255]
bytes("ab").push('é')               // Error: invalid_value: the value does not fit a single element (2 octets — use append)
bytes("ab").push("c")               // Error: invalid_argument_type — a sequence never reads as one element here

members.name: push_first
members.summary: Add each argument at the front as exactly one element, in argument order; see [`push`](kavun:type/bytes/push).

members.name: push_first_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `push_first`.

members.name: push_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `push`.

members.name: reduce
members.summary: Fold the elements left to right into an accumulator that starts at `init`.

doc.markdown:
The callback gets `(acc, element)`, or `(acc, index, element)` when it does not accept two arguments
([callbacks](kavun:type/bytes#callbacks)).

doc.code: bytes("abc").reduce(0, func(acc, x) { return acc + x.int() })           // => 294 — the checksum spelling

members.name: remove
members.summary: Remove every match of an element, a run, a set or a predicate; with no argument, the elements of the [blank set](kavun:type/bytes#the-blank-set).

doc.markdown:
A function argument gets the element, or `(index, element)` when it does not accept one argument
([callbacks](kavun:type/bytes#callbacks)).

`remove` and [`keep`](kavun:type/bytes/keep) both take the full menu and act on every occurrence; a miss is a silent no-op.

doc.code:
bytes("banana").keep(b'a')        // => bytes([97, 97, 97])
bytes("banana").remove("an")        // => bytes([98, 97])

members.name: remove_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `remove`.

members.name: remove_prefix
members.summary: Remove the element or run — or the longest of a set of them — once, anchored at the front; absent → unchanged.

doc.markdown:
The element or run is removed once — of a set, the longest that matches — and a miss answers the receiver
unchanged.

doc.code: bytes("foobar").remove_prefix("foo")        // => bytes([98, 97, 114])

members.name: remove_prefix_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `remove_prefix`.

members.name: remove_suffix
members.summary: Remove the element or run — or the longest of a set of them — once, anchored at the back; absent → unchanged; see [`remove_prefix`](kavun:type/bytes/remove_prefix).

members.name: remove_suffix_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `remove_suffix`.

members.name: repeat
members.summary: Concatenate the receiver with itself `n` times; `b * n` is the operator form.

doc.markdown: `repeat(n)` takes a whole-number count (`1.5` raises) and has the operator form `b * n` (no reflected `n * b`).

doc.code:
bytes("ab").repeat(2)           // => bytes([97, 98, 97, 98])
bytes("ab").repeat(1.5)         // Error: invalid_value — never silent truncation

members.name: replace
members.summary: Replace every occurrence of `old`, an element or a run, with `new`.

doc.markdown: Element or run in both positions; every occurrence, leftmost, non-overlapping.

members.name: replace_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `replace`.

members.name: reverse
members.summary: Reverse the order of the elements.

members.name: reverse_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `reverse`.

members.name: runes
members.summary: Decode the octets as `runes`; an octet that is not a symbol becomes its escape.

doc.code: bytes("hé").runes()         // => u"hé"

doc.markdown:
The `default` is taken for interface uniformity — every conversion carries it — and is never used: the
conversion is total.

members.name: slice
members.summary: Answer a copy of the elements from `start` to `end`; bounds **clamp** (contrast `splice`, which raises), negative indices count from the end.

doc.markdown: `slice(i, j)` **clamps**.

doc.code: bytes("abc").slice(1, 99)       // => bytes([98, 99]) — clamps

members.name: slice_view
members.summary: Answer the elements from `start` to `end` as a view sharing the receiver's storage, so mutation flows both ways.

doc.markdown: The sharing twin of [`slice`](kavun:type/bytes/slice).

doc.code:
sv := bytes("abcdef")
v := sv.slice_view(1, 3)        // shares storage
v[0] = b'X'                     // sv is now bytes([97, 88, 99, 100, 101, 102])

members.name: sort
members.summary: Sort the octets by value; there is no comparator.

doc.code: bytes("cba").sort()             // => bytes([97, 98, 99])

members.name: sort_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `sort`.

members.name: splice
members.summary: Removes `delete_count` elements at `start`, then inserts the items there.

doc.markdown:
`splice(start[, count, ...items])` is the positional edit: `start` outside `[0, len]` raises, a negative `count`
raises, the `count` clamps; the inserts take the add-side reading (runs spread, elements insert).

doc.code:
bytes("abcd").splice(1, 2, "XY")    // => bytes([97, 88, 89, 100])
bytes("ab").splice(3, 0)        // Error: index_out_of_bounds: (splice, start index) 3 out of range [0, 2]

members.name: splice_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `splice`.

members.name: split
members.summary: Split the octets into an array of the pieces between the separators.

doc.markdown:
Separators from the dispatch menu: element, run, homogeneous variadic set, element-level predicate, or absent
(= the blank set). **Explicit separators keep empty pieces** (n hits → n+1 pieces); the no-arg blank form drops
empties; an empty-run separator matches nothing. No limit argument exists. The pieces are `bytes`.

doc.code:
bytes("a,,b").split(b',')           // => [bytes([97]), bytes([]), bytes([98])] — empties kept
bytes("a::b").split("::")           // => [bytes([97]), bytes([98])]
bytes("a,b;c").split(b',', b';')    // => [bytes([97]), bytes([98]), bytes([99])]
bytes("a,b").split(b',', "::")      // Error: invalid_argument_type — mixed element + run set
bytes("a1b2c").split(func(x) { return x >= b'0' && x <= b'9' })
                                    // => [bytes([97]), bytes([98]), bytes([99])]
bytes("ab").split("")               // => [bytes([97, 98])] — an empty run matches nothing

members.name: split_lines
members.summary: Split the octets into an array of lines at `\n`, `\r\n` or `\r`; a trailing line break adds no empty last line.

doc.code: bytes("a\nb\r\nc").split_lines()    // => [bytes([97]), bytes([98]), bytes([99])]

members.name: string
members.summary: Decode the octets as a `string`; an octet that is not a symbol becomes its escape.

doc.code:
bytes("héllo").string()     // => "héllo"
bytes([255]).string()       // => "\xff" — the octet's escape — never raises, never loses it

doc.markdown:
The `default` is taken for interface uniformity — every conversion carries it — and is never used: the
conversion is total.

members.name: trim
members.summary: Repeatedly drop the elements at both ends while they belong to the set (the blank set with no argument).

doc.markdown:
A **set of elements**, stripped while they repeat at the edge; a run argument raises (the anchored run form is
`remove_prefix`/`remove_suffix`); no arguments = the blank set.

doc.code:
bytes("xxhixx").trim(b'x')          // => bytes([104, 105])
bytes("xyhi").trim("xy")            // Error: invalid_argument_type: trim takes a set of elements, not a run

members.name: trim_end
members.summary: Drop the trailing elements that belong to the set (the blank set with no argument); see [`trim`](kavun:type/bytes/trim).

members.name: trim_end_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `trim_end`.

members.name: trim_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `trim`.

members.name: trim_start
members.summary: Drop the leading elements that belong to the set (the blank set with no argument); see [`trim`](kavun:type/bytes/trim).

members.name: trim_start_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `trim_start`.

members.name: unique
members.summary: Drop repeats, keeping each element at its first occurrence.

doc.code: bytes("aabbaa").unique()        // => bytes([97, 98])

members.name: unique_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `unique`.

types.name: date
types.summary: A civil calendar day — `0001-01-01` … `9999-12-31` — with no clock and no zone.

doc.markdown:
## Overview

`date` is a domain scalar for the questions that are about *days*, not instants: a due date, a value date, a
birthday, the day a posting is booked. It has no time of day and no zone, so two dates compare and subtract
exactly, and nothing about them depends on where the script runs. When a day has to meet the clock, the
conversion names the zone (see [the time bridge](kavun:type/date#the-time-bridge)).

Key rules, each expanded below:

- Next to a `date`, a bare `int` **operand** is a number of **days**; a bare `int` in a **conversion** is a day
count since `1970-01-01` (epoch days). Operator = days, conversion = epoch days.
- One strict text form, `YYYY-MM-DD`, for `d"…"`, `date(s)`, `.string()`, f-strings and JSON. Any other text
shape names its layout: `date(s, layout)`, `s.parse_date(layout[, default])`.
- Month and year arithmetic states its end-of-month rule — `"clamp"` or `"last_day"` — with no default.
- `date` and `time` / `int` deliberately do **not** order against each other; `==` across them is `false`.

`date` values are immutable. A date is a primitive: it never allocates, and a `d"…"` literal is a compile-time
constant.

## Construction

doc.code:
d"2026-01-31"                       // literal: a compile-time constant; a bad literal is a compile error
date("2026-01-31")                  // the canonical text
date("31/01/2026", "%d/%m/%Y")      // a layout — the free form's second argument
"2026-01-31".date()                 // member form on text: the canonical text, as date(s) reads it
"31/01/2026".parse_date("%d/%m/%Y") // member form under a layout: the layout is required
"bad".parse_date("date", undefined) // => undefined — the default comes after the layout
date({year: 2026, month: 1, day: 31})   // components (every key optional, defaulting to date()'s part)
(20484).date()                      // epoch days: d"2026-01-31"
date(t"2026-03-31T23:30:00Z")       // a time's civil day, in the time's own zone
date()                              // => date("1970-01-01") — the zero value
undefined.date(d"2026-01-01")       // => date("2026-01-01") — the maybe-missing form

doc.markdown:
The text form is exactly `YYYY-MM-DD`: fixed width, a day that exists, nothing after it. Everything else raises
`conversion`; nothing normalizes:

doc.code:
date("2026-1-31")                   // Error: conversion: cannot convert string to date: expected a 2-digit month at offset 5
date("2026-02-30")                  // Error: conversion: ...: day 30 out of range 1..28
date("2026-01-31T00:00:00Z")        // Error: conversion: ...: unexpected text (a date has no clock or zone) at offset 10
date({year: 2026, month: 2, day: 29})   // Error: invalid_value: (date) day 29 out of range 1..28
date(3652059)                       // Error: conversion: cannot convert int to date — one day past 9999-12-31

doc.markdown:
**Layouts** for text are the `date` alias (the canonical form) or a `%`-template of **date directives**:
`%Y %m %d %e %j %B %b %A %a %n %t %%` (fixed width; English names, exact case; a weekday that contradicts the
date raises). Clock and zone directives (`%H %M %S %z` …) raise on a date, and so do the ambiguous `%y %Z` and
the week-based `%G %V %u %w %C`. A wrong layout raises `invalid_value` even when a default is given — it is a
mistake in the script, not a miss in the data:

doc.code:
date("Saturday 31 January 2026", "%A %d %B %Y")   // => date("2026-01-31")
date("2026-031", "%Y-%j")                         // => date("2026-01-31") — day of year
"x".parse_date("%H", undefined)                   // Error: invalid_value: directive %H is not available on a date
"x".parse_date("%d/%m/%Y", undefined)             // => undefined — the data missed, the layout is fine

doc.markdown:
## Operators

| expression | result | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `d + n` / `n + d` | `date` | `n` days later |
| `d - n` | `date` | `n` days earlier |
| `d2 - d1` | `int` | the days between (negative when `d2` is earlier) |
| `d1 < d2` (`<=` `>` `>=`) | `bool` | calendar order |
| `d == x` / `d != x` | `bool` | the same day; `false`/`true` against any non-date |
| a result outside `0001-01-01` … `9999-12-31` | raises | `invalid_value` |
| `n - d`, `d + d`, `d * n`, `d / n`, `d ± float` | raises | no meaning for a day |
| `d < n`, `d < t` (and the reverse) | raises | a day has no common order with a number or an instant |
| `d + t` | raises | a day is not a duration |

doc.code:
d := d"2026-01-31"
d + 1                       // => date("2026-02-01")
d - 31                      // => date("2025-12-31")
d"2026-03-01" - d"2026-02-01"   // => 28
d < d"2026-02-01"           // => true
d == 20484                  // => false — use d.int() == 20484
d < 5                       // Error: invalid_binary_operator: date < int
min(d, d"2026-02-01")       // => date("2026-01-31") — the global min/max work, the type has no min member

doc.markdown:
## The time bridge

A `date` has no zone, so every move to or from a `time` names one:

doc.code:
t := t"2026-03-31T23:30:00Z"
t.date()                       // => date("2026-03-31") — the civil day in the time's own zone
t.date_in("Europe/Kyiv")       // => date("2026-04-01") — the same instant is already April 1st in Kyiv
t.in_zone("Europe/Kyiv").date()  // => date("2026-04-01") — the same thing

d := d"2026-01-31"
d.time()                       // => time("2026-01-31T00:00:00Z") — midnight UTC; ≡ time(d)
d.time_in("Europe/Kyiv")       // => time("2026-01-31T00:00:00+02:00") — the start of the day in Kyiv

doc.markdown:
**Which day an instant falls on depends on the zone** — the first line above is a real hazard for bookings:
near midnight, UTC and local days differ. Name the zone the business day belongs to.

`time_in(zone)` answers the **first instant whose local date is the day**: midnight, or — on a day whose
midnight a daylight-saving change skips — the instant the gap ends. So `d.time_in(z).date_in(z) == d` always
holds:

`"Local"` and `""` are not zone names; an unknown zone raises.

## Conversions out

Every conversion is `x.T([default])`; each has its own entry.

`json.encode(d)` is `"2026-01-31"`; `json.decode` never produces a date (JSON has no date type), so a config
reads it back with `date(cfg.due)`. The binary codec is 4 bytes and re-validates the range on decode.

## For hosts

`kavun.ValueOf` accepts fin128's `civil.Date` directly, and a date's `Interface()` is a `civil.Date`.

members.name: add_days
members.summary: Move by `n` days, exactly `d + n`; see [`add_months`](kavun:type/date/add_months).

members.name: add_months
members.summary: Move by `n` calendar months with the end-of-month `rule`.

doc.markdown:
`add_days(n)` is `d + n`. Month and year steps take a **required** end-of-month rule, which only matters when
the start is a month end:

| rule | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `"clamp"` | keep the day of the month, clamped to the target month's length |
| `"last_day"` | a month-end start stays a month end |

members.name: add_years
members.summary: Move by `n` calendar years with the end-of-month `rule`; see [`add_months`](kavun:type/date/add_months).

members.name: array
members.summary: Answer a new one-element `array` holding the receiver.

doc.markdown: Total, so the default is never used.

members.name: components
members.summary: Answer the record `{year, month, day}`, the way back through `date(rec)`.

members.name: copy
members.summary: Answer the receiver — a `date` is always immutable.

doc.markdown: Identity no-ops on an immutable scalar, kept so generic code never type-errors.

members.name: date
members.summary: Answer the receiver, the identity conversion.

members.name: day
members.summary: Answer the day of the month.

members.name: days_in_month
members.summary: Answer the number of days in the month.

doc.markdown: For plain numbers — "how long is February 2027?" — ask a date in it: `d"2027-02-01".days_in_month()`.

members.name: days_in_year
members.summary: Answer the number of days in the year.

members.name: end_of_month
members.summary: Answer the last day of the month.

members.name: format
members.summary: Render the value per the [format mini-language](kavun:doc/format_mini_language).

doc.markdown:
The default render and `#date`/`#iso` are `YYYY-MM-DD`; a `%`-template takes the date directives
(`%Y %y %C %m %d %e %j %B %b %A %a %u %w %V %G %n %t %%`). Clock and zone directives, and the clock-bearing
aliases (`#datetime`, `#time`, `#unix`, …), raise:

doc.code:
d := d"2026-01-31"
f"{d}"                      // => "2026-01-31"
f"{d:#%d/%m/%Y}"            // => "31/01/2026"
f"{d:#%A %e %B %Y}"         // => "Saturday 31 January 2026"
f"{d:v}"                    // `date("2026-01-31")` — the source form
d.format("#%H")             // Error: formatting: directive %H is not available on a date

members.name: freeze
members.summary: Answer the receiver — a `date` is always immutable; see [`copy`](kavun:type/date/copy).

members.name: int
members.summary: Answer the epoch days, the count since `1970-01-01`.

doc.code:
d := d"2026-01-31"
d.int()                     // => 20484 — epoch days; (20484).date() is the way back

members.name: is_end_of_month
members.summary: Report whether the day is the last of its month.

doc.code:
f := d"2028-02-10"
f.is_end_of_month()  // => false

members.name: is_leap_year
members.summary: Report whether the year is a leap year.

doc.code:
f := d"2028-02-10"
f.is_leap_year()     // => true

members.name: is_true
members.summary: Report truthiness: `date()`, `1970-01-01`, is falsy (`!!x` ⟺ `x != date()`).

doc.markdown:
Derived like every type's: `date()` (`1970-01-01`) is falsy, every other day is truthy — including `0001-01-01`
and `9999-12-31`, the sentinels other systems use for "unset" and "no end". A host that means "missing" by one
should map it to `undefined`.

members.name: month
members.summary: Answer the month, 1–12 (January is 1).

doc.code:
d := d"2026-01-31"
d.month()            // => 1 — January is 1

doc.code:

types.name: decimal
types.summary: 128-bit base-10 decimals (dec128) for exact monetary arithmetic.

doc.markdown:
## Overview

`decimal` is a 128-bit decimal floating-point number: up to 38 significant digits with a fractional scale of 0 to
19 digits. Arithmetic is exact in base 10 — `0.1d + 0.2d == 0.3d` is `true`, where the float spelling is famously
`false`. Money and anything else that must be exact in base 10 belongs in `decimal`; measurements and physics
belong in [`float`](kavun:type/float).

`decimal` belongs to the numeric family alongside [`int`](kavun:type/int) and `float`: it pairs with `int` in arithmetic
and compares exactly against both. It has no Inf representation at all (`is_inf()` is constantly `false`), and a
NaN exists only as an error state a **host** can hand in — no operation in the language produces one, because
every path that would raises instead (see [NaN as an error state](kavun:type/decimal#nan-as-an-error-state)).

## Literals and construction

A base-10 numeric literal with a `d` suffix is a decimal:

doc.code:
price = 19.99d
two = 2d
neg = -2.5d        // unary minus, exact
big = 1.5e3d       // => 1500d — exponent form, same value and scale as decimal("1.5e3")

doc.markdown:
The free `decimal(x)` constructor (equivalently `x.decimal()`) converts and parses; the member's optional
`x.decimal(default)` rescues bad data:

doc.code:
decimal()                  // => 0d — the zero value
decimal("0.1")             // => 0.1d — parsing text is the lossless entry point
decimal(3)                 // => 3d
decimal(1.5)               // => 1.5d — from float, shortest decimal reading
decimal("abc")             // Error: conversion: cannot convert string to decimal — parse raises, no NaN sentinel
"abc".decimal(0d)          // => 0d — the member's default rescues bad data
undefined.decimal(0d)      // => 0d — the maybe-missing form
decimal("inf")             // Error: conversion: cannot convert string to decimal — the type has no Inf
decimal("1e3")             // => 1000d — scientific notation parses, in either case ("1E3" too)

doc.markdown:
### Scientific notation and scale

Both the mantissa's own digits and the exponent contribute to the resulting scale, so the notation carries
precision rather than discarding it:

doc.code:
decimal("1.0e-3").format("s")   // => "0.0010" — scale 4: mantissa scale 1, shifted 3 more places
decimal("2.5E2").scale()        // => 0 — 250d; the exponent absorbed the fractional digit
decimal("1e-25")                // Error: conversion: cannot convert string to decimal — past the scale-19 ceiling

doc.markdown:
## Arithmetic and operators

| operator | meaning | notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `+` `-` `*` | add, subtract, multiply | exact; raise `invalid_value` past 38 digits |
| `/` | division | up to 19 places; an exact quotient keeps its natural scale (`10d / 4d` → `2.5d`); `/ 0d` raises `division_by_zero` |
| `%` | remainder | `10d % 3d` → `1d`; `% 0d` raises `division_by_zero` |
| `-x` | negation | exact, never overflows |

doc.code:
0.1d + 0.2d            // => 0.3d — exact
0.1d + 0.2d == 0.3d    // => true
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3       // => false — the float contrast
1d / 3d                // => 0.3333333333333333333d — 19 fractional digits

doc.markdown:
### Scale of a result

Each value carries a scale (count of stored fractional digits, observable via `scale()` and `format("s")`).
Addition keeps the wider operand's scale and multiplication adds scales. Division answers up to 19 places, but an
**exact** quotient keeps its natural scale — the dividend's scale minus the divisor's, or 0 — so it does not
sprout trailing zeros:

doc.code:
(decimal("0.10") + decimal("0.20")).format("s")    // => "0.30" — scale 2
(decimal("1.5") * decimal("2.00")).scale()          // => 3 — scales add
(decimal("10.00") / 4d).format("s")                 // => "2.50" — exact, natural scale 2 - 0
(1d / 2d).format("s")                               // => "0.5"
(1d / 3d).scale()                                   // => 19 — inexact, so every place is used

doc.markdown:
A `d`-suffixed literal carries the scale it was written with, and two literals that differ only in trailing
zeros are two different constants:

doc.code:
(1.5d).scale()     // => 1
(1.50d).scale()    // => 2
1.5d == 1.50d      // => true — numeric equality is scale-blind

doc.markdown:
Use `round(n, mode)` to pin a result to a scale, `rescale(n)` to change the scale without changing the value,
and `canonical()` to drop trailing zeros.

### Rounding at the precision ceiling

A decimal holds up to 38 significant digits with at most 19 fractional places. When an exact result does not
fit, the scale is reduced to the largest that still holds the integer part, and the discarded digits are
**truncated toward zero — not reported**:

This is ordinary and expected, and it is the same rule as `int`'s `1 / 2 == 0`: a decimal moves in steps of its
smallest unit, and a result finer than that step cannot be held. No fixed-point type can represent a third, and
the same ceiling applies to a very small product. The result does not record that digits were lost; only a
result whose *integer* part does not fit raises (see [Overflow raises](kavun:type/decimal#overflow-raises)).

The practical answer is to keep intermediates wide and round **once, at the boundary**, stating the scale and
the rounding mode at each point a result is pinned down: `round(2, mode)`, `div_round(y, 2, mode)` and the rest
of the [`*_round` members](kavun:type/decimal#arithmetic-straight-to-a-scale--the-_round-members). A calculation carried at a
working scale well below 19 is unaffected by the ceiling. To check that a value is *already* on a grid without
changing it, `rescale(n)` raises instead of dropping a digit.

### Overflow raises

A result that no longer fits 128 bits raises a catchable `invalid_value` error:

### Division by zero

`x / 0d` and `x % 0d` raise `division_by_zero`, the same kind `int` answers for `1 / 0`. There is nothing to
check after the division:

doc.code:
1d / 0d              // Error: division_by_zero: division by zero
0d / 0d              // Error: division_by_zero: division by zero
1d % 0d              // Error: division_by_zero: division by zero

doc.markdown:
### decimal never mixes with float

Arithmetic between `decimal` and `float` raises — there is no silently-chosen loser of precision. Convert
explicitly on the side you mean:

doc.code:
1.5d + 1.0    // Error: invalid_binary_operator: decimal + float
1.5 + 1d      // Error: invalid_binary_operator: float + decimal
1.5d + 1      // => 2.5d — int pairs fine
1.5d * 2      // => 3.0d — the scale rides along
1.5d + (1.0).decimal()    // => 2.5d — explicit, decimal wins

doc.markdown:
Comparisons across the pair are allowed (and exact) — see below.

## NaN as an error state

dec128 signals every failure the same way — it answers NaN — and Kavun treats that as an **error state, not a
value**. Unlike an IEEE NaN it even compares equal to itself, so it behaves as an ordinary number everywhere
downstream and a wrong answer would propagate silently through a whole script.

So **no operation in the language produces one**. Every path that would raises instead:

doc.code:
x := 99999999999999999999d   // 20 significant digits
decimal("abc")       // Error: conversion — the parse
1d / 0d              // Error: division_by_zero
0d % 0d              // Error: division_by_zero
(-1d).sqrt()         // Error: invalid_value: (sqrt) square root of negative number
x * x                // Error: invalid_value: (*) overflow  — past the 128-bit coefficient
(1e39).decimal()     // Error: conversion — the float is finite but too large for dec128

doc.markdown:
That mirrors `float`, whose arithmetic already raises on a NaN or ±Inf result.

`is_nan()` and `error_details()` remain because a **host** can bind a NaN decimal through the embedding API —
nothing in the language can. For a decimal a script produced, `is_nan()` is always `false` and
`error_details()` is always `undefined`. On a host-supplied NaN:

doc.code:
n.is_nan()           // => true
n.error_details()    // => error("...") — why this NaN exists
n.is_true()          // Error: invalid_value: decimal NaN is neither true nor false in a boolean context
n.int()              // Error: conversion: cannot convert decimal to int
n.sign()             // => 0
doc.reason: needs a NaN decimal, which only a host can bind

doc.markdown:
In comparisons such a NaN follows the numeric family's total order: the unique minimum, equal only to another
NaN, so sorting stays deterministic.

## Comparisons and cross-type pairing

`==` and the orderings are **exact mathematical comparisons**. Trailing zeros never matter — equality compares
numeric value, not scale:

doc.code:
2.50d == 2.5d      // => true — scale is representation, not identity
1d == 1            // => true
1d < 1.5           // => true — float comparison is allowed (only arithmetic is refused)
0.1d == 0.1        // => false — float 0.1 is really 0.1000000000000000055511…
0.1d < 0.1         // => true — exactly below the float's true value
(0.1).decimal() == 0.1d    // => true — the float's shortest decimal reading is 0.1

doc.markdown:
`bool` / `byte` / `rune` widen to their integer value. Equality against a `string` compares the decimal's own text
form, which carries its scale; ordering against text raises:

doc.code:
decimal("1.50") == "1.50"    // => true — the scale is part of the rendering
decimal("1.50") == "1.5"     // => false — a different text, though the same NUMBER
decimal("1.50") == 1.5d      // => true — numeric equality is scale-blind, text equality is not

doc.markdown:
## Rounding modes

Every member that rounds takes the **mode as a string**, because in a real application the rounding rule is
configuration, not code. The seven names are Python's `decimal` modes, lowercased and without the `ROUND_`
prefix — so `down` means *toward zero*, as it does in Python, and the directions toward −∞ / +∞ are `floor` /
`ceiling`:

| mode | rule | `2.5d` → 0 | `-2.5d` → 0 | `2.345d` → 2 | `-2.345d` → 2 | Python |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `"ceiling"` | toward +∞ | `3d` | `-2d` | `2.35d` | `-2.34d` | `ROUND_CEILING` |
| `"floor"` | toward −∞ | `2d` | `-3d` | `2.34d` | `-2.35d` | `ROUND_FLOOR` |
| `"down"` | toward zero (truncate) | `2d` | `-2d` | `2.34d` | `-2.34d` | `ROUND_DOWN` |
| `"up"` | away from zero | `3d` | `-3d` | `2.35d` | `-2.35d` | `ROUND_UP` |
| `"half_down"` | nearest, ties toward zero | `2d` | `-2d` | `2.34d` | `-2.34d` | `ROUND_HALF_DOWN` |
| `"half_up"` | nearest, ties away from zero ("schoolbook") | `3d` | `-3d` | `2.35d` | `-2.35d` | `ROUND_HALF_UP` |
| `"half_even"` | nearest, ties to even (banker's) | `2d` | `-2d` | `2.34d` | `-2.34d` | `ROUND_HALF_EVEN` |

The name must match exactly — lowercase, no prefix. Anything else raises and lists the valid names; there is no
fallback mode:

doc.code:
(1d).round(2, "bank")               // Error: invalid_value: (round) unknown rounding mode "bank", expected one of: ceiling, floor, down, up, half_down, half_up, half_even
(1d).round(2, "ROUND_HALF_EVEN")    // Error: invalid_value: (round) unknown rounding mode "ROUND_HALF_EVEN", …
(1d).round(2, 3)                    // Error: invalid_argument_type: (round) argument mode expects type string, got int

doc.markdown:
## Arithmetic straight to a scale — the `*_round` members

Every member whose last two arguments are `(scale, mode)` ends in `_round`. Each performs its operation with the
intermediate held **exactly** and makes **one** rounding decision, landing on exactly the requested scale — where
composing an operator with `round` rounds twice (once at the 19-place ceiling, once at `round`) and keeps the
operator's scale. The other operands are `decimal` or `int`, the domain the `/` and `*` operators accept; `float`
is refused here for the same reason it is refused there.

| member | computes | typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `div_round(y, n, mode)` | `x / y` | a rate per period |
| `mul_round(y, n, mode)` | `x * y` | a line item |
| `mul_percent_round(r, n, mode)` | `x * r / 100` | VAT, fees — the division by 100 is a move of the point |
| `mul_add_round(b, c, n, mode)` | `x * b + c` | principal × rate + fee |
| `mul_div_round(b, c, n, mode)` | `x * b / c` | proration, day counts (31/365) |
| `sqrt_round(n, mode)` | `√x` | |
| `pow_round(k, n, mode)` | `x^k`, integer `k` | compounding — computed with guard digits |
| `nth_root_round(k, n, mode)` | `x^(1/k)` | the monthly factor of an annual rate |
| `pow_rational_round(p, q, n, mode)` | `x^(p/q)` | five months of a yearly rate |
| `exp_round(n, mode)`, `ln_round(n, mode)` | `eˣ`, `ln x` | continuous compounding |
| `log10_round(n, mode)`, `log2_round(n, mode)` | `log₁₀ x`, `log₂ x` | |

doc.code:
(10d).div_round(4d, 2, "half_even")                 // => 2.50d — a money result carrying its cents
10d / 4d                                            // => 2.5d — the operator keeps the natural scale
(7d).div_round(3, 2, "up")                          // => 2.34d
(100.00d).mul_percent_round(7.5d, 2, "half_even")   // => 7.50d
(250000.00d).mul_add_round(0.0425d, 12.345d, 2, "half_even")   // => 10637.34d — 10637.345 is an exact tie
(1000d).mul_div_round(31, 365, 2, "half_up")        // => 84.93d — one rounding on the exact numerator
(2d).sqrt_round(4, "half_even")                     // => 1.4142d
(1.000164383561643836d).pow_round(3650, 19, "half_up")   // => 1.8220289545384488980d — ten years of daily rests
(1.126825d).nth_root_round(12, 10, "half_up")       // => 1.0099999977d
(1.06d).pow_rational_round(5, 12, 19, "half_up")    // => 1.0245758393924285985d
(-8d).pow_rational_round(2, 6, 0, "half_up")        // => -2d — 2/6 is reduced to 1/3 first
(1d).exp_round(10, "half_even")                     // => 2.7182818285d
(1000d).log10_round(4, "half_even")                 // => 3.0000d — an exact power of the base is exact

doc.markdown:
`mul_div_round` is the one of these that cannot be composed at all: scaling by a ratio whose decimal expansion
never ends (1/3, 31/365) has no exact decimal factor to multiply by first. `pow_round` against `pow`: `pow(k)`
truncates at the 19-place ceiling at every step of the power, `pow_round` carries guard digits and rounds once, so
over thousands of periods they can differ in the last places. `nth_root_round` and `pow_rational_round` are
**correctly rounded**; `exp_round`, `ln_round`, `log10_round` and `log2_round` are the only members that are not
exact — they are **faithfully rounded**, within one unit in the last place of the correctly rounded value.

All of them raise rather than answering a sentinel:

doc.code:
(1d).div_round(0d, 2, "up")                  // Error: division_by_zero
(1d).mul_div_round(1, 0, 2, "up")            // Error: division_by_zero
(0d).pow_round(-1, 4, "half_up")             // Error: division_by_zero
(-2d).sqrt_round(2, "half_even")             // Error: invalid_value: (sqrt_round) square root of negative number
(0d).ln_round(4, "half_even")                // Error: invalid_value: (ln_round) argument outside the domain of the function
(-4d).nth_root_round(2, 2, "half_up")        // Error: invalid_value: (nth_root_round) argument outside the domain of the function
(4d).nth_root_round(16385, 2, "half_up")     // Error: invalid_value: (nth_root_round) degree must be at most 16384, got 16385
(1d).div_round(3.0, 2, "up")                 // Error: invalid_argument_type: (div_round) argument first expects type decimal or int, got float
(1d).div_round(3d, 20, "up")                 // Error: invalid_value: (div_round) scale must be between 0 and 19

doc.markdown:
The degree limit (and the same limit on a reduced `p` or `q` of `pow_rational_round`) is a cost ceiling: 16384
covers 40 years of daily rests.

## Allocating an amount

`allocate` and `allocate_equal` divide an amount into shares that **sum to exactly the amount** — a reconciliation is an
equality, not a tolerance. Both answer a new, mutable array.

| member | shares | the leftover quanta go to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `allocate_equal(k, n)` | `k` equal shares at scale `n` | the shares with the largest remainders, ties to the lowest index |
| `allocate(ratios, n)` | proportional to `ratios` (an array of `decimal`/`int`) | the same |
| `allocate_equal_residual(k, n, index, mode)` | every share rounded with `mode` … | … except the one at `index`, which takes what is left |
| `allocate_residual(ratios, n, index, mode)` | the same, proportionally | the same |

The `_residual` forms are the convention of an amortization schedule or a syndicated facility: the last
installment, or the lead bank, absorbs the rounding. `index` counts from the end when negative, as an array index
does.

The target scale must be at least the amount's own: allocating 1.005 into cents would have to round first, and
the allocation refuses to do that silently.

doc.code:
(1.005d).allocate_equal(3, 2)                      // Error: invalid_value: (allocate_equal) scale 2 is below the amount's own scale 3; round the amount first
(1.005d).round(2, "half_even").allocate_equal(3, 2) // => [0.34d, 0.33d, 0.33d]
(1d).allocate_equal(0, 2)                          // Error: invalid_value: (allocate_equal) argument count must be positive, got 0
(1000.00d).allocate_equal_residual(7, 2, 7, "half_up") // Error: index_out_of_bounds: (allocate_equal_residual) 7 out of range [0, 6]
(100d).allocate([1, -1], 2)                        // Error: invalid_value: (allocate) ratio at index 1 is negative
(100d).allocate([0, 0], 2)                         // Error: invalid_value: (allocate) ratios must not all be zero
(100d).allocate([], 2)                             // Error: invalid_value: (allocate) ratios must not be empty

doc.markdown:
## No sequence members

Scalars have no `len()`, no elements, and no `repeat`:

doc.code: (1.5d).repeat(2)    // Error: invalid_method: type decimal has no method repeat

doc.markdown:
## Conversions

`x.T()` answers a valid `T` or raises (kind `conversion`); `x.T(default)` answers the default instead;
`undefined.T(d)` → `d` covers maybe-missing data.

| target | behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `decimal` | identity |
| `int` | truncation toward zero for in-range values (documented resolution loss); out-of-range and NaN raise-or-default |
| `float` | nearest float64 — approximate by nature |
| `bool` | zero test; NaN raises-or-defaults |
| `string` / `runes` | rendering at the value's own scale, no `d` suffix (total — the default is never used); `canonical()` first for the trimmed reading |
| `time` | unix timestamp as sec.frac, **exact to the nanosecond** |

There is no `byte()` or `rune()` conversion — `int` is the sole gateway to the ordinal scalars
(`x.int().byte()`).
