`f` / `F` (fixed, default precision 6, rounds half-away-from-zero), `s` (the explicit spelling of the default),
`%` (×100 with percent sign), `e` / `E` (scientific, default precision 6), `g` / `G` (the shorter of the two
readings, fixed and scientific). The `v` verb shows the literal form with the `d` suffix, scale included, so it
round-trips.

**Scientific output is exact.** The digits come from the decimal's own coefficient, so a precision past the
17th significant digit shows the value rather than the nearest `float64`:

Ties round half away from zero, like the `f` verb: `(8.5d).format(".0e")` is `"9e+00"`. A `g` precision counts
**significant** digits, not fractional ones — `(2d/3d).format(".5g")` is `"0.66667"`.

The `!` flag is the trimmed reading, accepted **only** on the default verb and `s` — everywhere else a precision
already governs the digits, and `!` is a parse error:

doc.code:
(1.500d).format()           // => "1.500"
(1.500d).format("s")        // => "1.500" — same thing, said explicitly
(1.500d).format("!")        // => "1.5"
(1.500d).format("v")        // => "1.500d"
(1234.5d).format(",.2f")    // => "1,234.50"
(0.125d).format(".1%")      // => "12.5%"
(1.5d).format("+.2f")       // => "+1.50"
(1.500d).format(".2!f")     // Error: unsupported_format_spec: type decimal does not support format spec ".2!f"

doc.markdown: A precision past the 19-place ceiling pads with zeros — a decimal has no digits there, so writing them is exact:

The `f`, `%` and `e` verbs round **for display**, always half away from zero. A business rounding rule belongs in
the value, before formatting — `f"{total.round(2, rule):,.2f}"` — so the stored number and the printed one agree
whatever the rule is.

members.name: freeze
members.summary: Answer the receiver — a `decimal` is always immutable; see [`copy`](kavun:type/decimal/copy).

members.name: int
members.summary: Truncate toward zero to an `int`; out-of-range values and NaN raise unless a default is given.

doc.code:
(1.9d).int()      // => 1 — truncation toward zero
(-1.9d).int()     // => -1
decimal("100000000000000000000").int()     // Error: conversion: cannot convert decimal to int
decimal("100000000000000000000").int(0)    // => 0

members.name: integer_digits
members.summary: Answer the number of digits before the point.

doc.code:
(-123.45d).integer_digits()       // => 3
(0.99d).integer_digits()          // => 0

members.name: is_inf
members.summary: Report whether the value is infinite — always `false` on a `decimal`.

doc.code: (1.5d).is_inf()          // => false — ALWAYS — the type has no Inf representation

doc.markdown:
`is_nan()` / `is_inf()` exist on every numeric type so generic code never type-switches; on `decimal`, `is_inf()`
is the constant-`false` end of that contract.

members.name: is_integer
members.summary: Report whether the value has no fractional part.

doc.code:
(1.000d).is_integer()             // => true — nothing after the point but zeros
(1.5d).is_integer()               // => false

members.name: is_nan
members.summary: Report whether the value is NaN, which only a host can supply; see [NaN as an error state](kavun:type/decimal#nan-as-an-error-state).

doc.code: (1.5d).is_nan()          // => false

members.name: is_negative
members.summary: Report whether the value is less than zero.

doc.code: (-1.5d).is_negative()    // => true

members.name: is_positive
members.summary: Report whether the value is greater than zero.

doc.code: (1.5d).is_positive()     // => true

members.name: is_true
members.summary: Report truthiness, which is inequality with zero: `!!x` ⟺ `x != 0d`; NaN raises.

doc.markdown: Inequality with zero, member and free spelling alike; NaN raises:

doc.code:
(0d).is_true()      // => false
(0.5d).is_true()    // => true
is_true(0d)         // => false
1d / 0d             // Error: division_by_zero — there is no decimal NaN to ask about

members.name: is_zero
members.summary: Report whether the value is zero.

doc.code: (0d).is_zero()           // => true — scale-blind: 0.00d is zero too

members.name: ln_round
members.summary: Answer the natural logarithm, rounding once to scale `n` with `mode`; see [the `*_round` members](kavun:type/decimal#arithmetic-straight-to-a-scale--the-_round-members).

members.name: log10_round
members.summary: Answer the base-10 logarithm, rounding once to scale `n` with `mode`; see [the `*_round` members](kavun:type/decimal#arithmetic-straight-to-a-scale--the-_round-members).

members.name: log2_round
members.summary: Answer the base-2 logarithm, rounding once to scale `n` with `mode`; see [the `*_round` members](kavun:type/decimal#arithmetic-straight-to-a-scale--the-_round-members).

members.name: mul_add_round
members.summary: Answer `x * b + c`, rounding once to scale `n` with `mode`; see [the `*_round` members](kavun:type/decimal#arithmetic-straight-to-a-scale--the-_round-members).

members.name: mul_div_round
members.summary: Answer `x * b / c`, rounding once to scale `n` with `mode`; see [the `*_round` members](kavun:type/decimal#arithmetic-straight-to-a-scale--the-_round-members).

members.name: mul_percent_round
members.summary: Answer `x * r / 100`, rounding once to scale `n` with `mode`; see [the `*_round` members](kavun:type/decimal#arithmetic-straight-to-a-scale--the-_round-members).

members.name: mul_round
members.summary: Multiply by `y`, rounding once to scale `n` with `mode`; see [the `*_round` members](kavun:type/decimal#arithmetic-straight-to-a-scale--the-_round-members).

members.name: negate
members.summary: Answer the value with its sign flipped.

doc.code: (2.5d).negate()     // => -2.5d — the member spelling of unary minus

members.name: next_down
members.summary: Answer the value one unit in the last place of its current scale down; see [`next_up`](kavun:type/decimal/next_up).

doc.code: decimal("1.50").next_down()    // => 1.49d

members.name: next_up
members.summary: Answer the value one unit in the last place of its current scale up.

doc.code:
(1d).next_up()      // => 2d — one unit in the last place of the CURRENT scale…
decimal("1.50").next_up()      // => 1.51d — …so the step depends on scale

members.name: nth_root_round
members.summary: Answer the `k`-th root, rounding once to scale `n` with `mode`; see [the `*_round` members](kavun:type/decimal#arithmetic-straight-to-a-scale--the-_round-members).

members.name: pow
members.summary: Raise the value to the integer `exponent`.

doc.code:
(2d).pow(10)        // => 1024d — integer exponent
(2d).pow(-1)        // => 0.5000000000000000000d — a negative exponent is the reciprocal, taken at 19 places
(1.50d).pow(2)      // => 2.2500d — the scale multiplies: scale(base) x n
(0d).pow(-1)        // Error: division_by_zero
(10d).pow(39)       // Error: invalid_value: (pow) overflow — 10d.pow(38) is the largest that fits

members.name: pow_rational_round
members.summary: Raise the value to `p/q`, rounding once to scale `n` with `mode`; see [the `*_round` members](kavun:type/decimal#arithmetic-straight-to-a-scale--the-_round-members).

members.name: pow_round
members.summary: Raise the value to the integer `k`, rounding once to scale `n` with `mode`; see [the `*_round` members](kavun:type/decimal#arithmetic-straight-to-a-scale--the-_round-members).

members.name: quo_rem
members.summary: Answer `[quotient, remainder]` of division by `y`, the quotient truncated toward zero.

doc.code:
(-7.5d).quo_rem(2)               // => [-3d, -1.5d] — quotient truncated toward zero, as Python's divmod on Decimal
q, r := (17d).quo_rem(5)         // q = 3d, r = 2d; q * y + r == x exactly
(1d).quo_rem(0)                  // Error: division_by_zero

members.name: rescale
members.summary: Change the scale to `n` without changing the value; a value that would change raises.

doc.markdown:
`rescale(n)` changes the scale **without changing the value**: it pads, and it narrows only when the digits it
drops are zeros. A value that would change raises — `round(n, mode)` is the spelling that changes it, and it
names how. That makes `rescale(n)` the check that a value is already on a grid:

doc.code:
(1.5d).rescale(3).format("s")     // => "1.500"
(1.500d).rescale(1).format("s")   // => "1.5" — only zeros dropped
(1.55d).rescale(1)                // Error: invalid_value: (rescale) 1.55 has non-zero digits past scale 1; use round(n, mode) to round it
(1.5d).rescale(40)                // Error: invalid_value: (rescale) scale must be between 0 and 19

members.name: round
members.summary: Round to `n` fractional places with the rounding `mode`.

doc.markdown:
`round(n, mode)` answers **exactly** `n` fractional places — the shape a monetary result needs, and what Python's
`round(Decimal, n)` answers. A negative `n` rounds to tens, hundreds, … and answers a whole number:

doc.code:
rule = "half_even"                     // typically read from configuration
(2.345d).round(2, rule)                // => 2.34d
(1.5d).round(2, rule).format("s")      // => "1.50" — exactly two places, padded
(1234.5d).round(-2, rule)              // => 1200d
(2.5d).round(-1, "half_up")            // => 0d
(1d).round(20, "up")                   // Error: invalid_value: (round) places must be between -38 and 19

doc.markdown:
Each mode also has a **twin** that spells it in the name, for the common case where the rule is fixed:
`round_ceiling(n)`, `round_floor(n)`, `round_down(n)`, `round_up(n)`, `round_half_down(n)`, `round_half_up(n)`,
`round_half_even(n)`. A twin answers exactly what `round(n, "<mode>")` answers:

doc.code:
(2.345d).round_half_up(2)     // => 2.35d — same as (2.345d).round(2, "half_up")
(2.4d).round_ceiling(0)       // => 3d — a direction applies to any fraction, not just ties
(-2.9d).round_down(0)         // => -2d — toward zero

doc.markdown:
There is **no plain `round()` with a default mode, no `floor()`, `ceil()` or `trunc()`**: every rounding states
its mode. Floor is `round_floor(0)`, ceiling `round_ceiling(0)`, truncation `round_down(n)`.

members.name: round_ceiling
members.summary: Round to `n` fractional places, toward +∞; see [`round`](kavun:type/decimal/round).

members.name: round_down
members.summary: Round to `n` fractional places, toward zero; see [`round`](kavun:type/decimal/round).

members.name: round_floor
members.summary: Round to `n` fractional places, toward −∞; see [`round`](kavun:type/decimal/round).

members.name: round_half_down
members.summary: Round to `n` fractional places, ties toward zero; see [`round`](kavun:type/decimal/round).

members.name: round_half_even
members.summary: Round to `n` fractional places, ties to even; see [`round`](kavun:type/decimal/round).

members.name: round_half_up
members.summary: Round to `n` fractional places, ties away from zero; see [`round`](kavun:type/decimal/round).

members.name: round_significant
members.summary: Round to at most `k` significant digits with the rounding `mode`.

doc.code:
(1.09875d).round_significant(5, "half_even")   // => 1.0988d — at most 5 significant digits, an FX quote
(9.99d).round_significant(2, "half_up")        // => 10.0d — the carry adds a digit no scale can drop

members.name: round_to_multiple
members.summary: Round to a multiple of `m` with the rounding `mode`.

doc.code:
(2.37d).round_to_multiple(0.05d, "half_up")    // => 2.35d — Swiss/Swedish cash rounding; the result has m's scale
(183.47d).round_to_multiple(10, "ceiling")     // => 190d — "the next whole 10"
(2.37d).round_to_multiple(0, "half_up")        // Error: invalid_value: (round_to_multiple) the multiple must be positive, got 0

members.name: round_up
members.summary: Round to `n` fractional places, away from zero; see [`round`](kavun:type/decimal/round).

members.name: runes
members.summary: Render the value at its own scale as `runes`; see [`string`](kavun:type/decimal/string).

members.name: scale
members.summary: Answer the scale, the number of stored fractional digits.

doc.code: decimal("1.50").scale()        // => 2 — stored fractional digits

members.name: scale_by_pow10
members.summary: Multiply by 10ⁿ as a move of the point, never rounded.

doc.code:
(5.25d).scale_by_pow10(-2)       // => 0.0525d — a percent to a fraction, as a move of the point, never rounded
(1.5d).scale_by_pow10(3)         // => 1500d
(1d).scale_by_pow10(60)          // Error: invalid_value: (scale_by_pow10) overflow

members.name: sign
members.summary: Answer the sign as an `int`: `-1`, `0` or `1`.

doc.code: (-2.5d).sign()      // => -1 — an int; 0 for zero, 1 for positive

members.name: significant_digits
members.summary: Answer the number of significant digits, trailing zeros included.

doc.code: (1.50d).significant_digits()      // => 3 — trailing zeros are digits of the representation

members.name: sqrt
members.summary: Answer the square root.

doc.code:
(2d).sqrt()         // => 1.4142135623730950488d
(-1d).sqrt()        // Error: invalid_value: (sqrt) square root of negative number

members.name: sqrt_round
members.summary: Answer the square root, rounding once to scale `n` with `mode`; see [the `*_round` members](kavun:type/decimal#arithmetic-straight-to-a-scale--the-_round-members).

members.name: string
members.summary: Render the value at its own scale, without the `d` suffix, as a `string`.

doc.code:
(1.50d).string()  // => "1.50" — the scale rides along
(1.50d).canonical().string()   // => "1.5" — the trimmed reading
decimal("1.50").string()       // => "1.50" — every rendering carries the scale

doc.markdown:
The `default` is taken for interface uniformity — every conversion carries it — and is never used: the
conversion is total.

members.name: time
members.summary: Read the value as a unix timestamp in seconds, exact to the nanosecond.

doc.markdown:
A decimal in conversion context is a unix timestamp read as `seconds.fraction` — the **exact** path, unlike
`float`'s (dec128 is base-10, so every digit survives to the nanosecond):

types.name: dict
types.summary: Mutable string-keyed maps.

doc.markdown:
## Overview

**A dict is a set of keys, each with an attached value: the key is the element, the value is the attachment.**
That one sentence generates the whole surface. Search members (`contains`, `count`, `index`, `any`, `all`) match
keys; `keys()` and `values()` name the two axes; `keep`/`remove` keep or drop whole entries; `map` transforms
the attachment with the keys fixed. Any operation that would have to choose between the key axis and the value
axis is deliberately absent — instead you name the collection you mean: `d.values().contains(x)`,
`d.values().sum()`, `d.keys().min()`.

Dicts are reference-typed: `b = a` shares the underlying map, `copy()` makes an independent one — see
[container semantics](kavun:doc/container_semantics). Keys are always strings. Values can be anything.

`dict` and [`record`](kavun:type/record) are the same map shape with two access grammars: on a `dict`, `d[k]` is
element access and `d.name(...)` is a member-function call; on a `record`, `r.k` is field access and there are no
member functions at all. Conversions between them are one call in either direction (see [`record()`](kavun:type/dict/record) and
[`dict()`](kavun:type/dict/dict)).

The two failure modes shared by the surface:

- Every `_in_place` twin raises `not_mutable` on a frozen receiver; on success it mutates the shared map and
returns the receiver, so mutators chain.
- Every member that takes an argument has **no blank (no-argument) reading**: a map has two axes, so a bare
`d.keep()` / `d.contains()` / `d.any()` has no single meaning and raises `wrong_num_arguments` rather than
guessing one.

There is **no `.string()`** on dict, and the free `string(d)` raises too — a map's content has no text form.
The rendering is `format()` / f-strings.

## Literals and construction

There is no dict literal — `{a: 1}` is a [record](kavun:type/record) literal. A dict is built by the `dict()`
constructor:

doc.code:
d = dict({a: 1, b: 2})       // from a record literal: dict({"a": 1, "b": 2})
q = dict({"x y": 1})         // string key form for keys that aren't identifiers
e = dict()                   // empty dict — a real, writable map:
e["x"] = 1
e                            // => dict({"x": 1})

// a dict argument is copied, never aliased — a constructor constructs
c = dict(d)                  // a new, independent dict (shallow: values are shared)
c["a"] = 9                   // d["a"] is still 1
dict(freeze(d))              // mutable again

doc.markdown:
### The entries form

`dict([[k, v], ...])` constructs from a list of entries, where each element must be exactly a 2-element array —
anything else raises (`conversion`). Keys go through their own string conversion; a duplicate key is
last-one-wins. `arr.dict()` is the same reading as a member on `array`:

doc.code:
dict([["a", 1], ["b", 2]])       // => dict({"a": 1, "b": 2})
[["a", 1], ["b", 2]].dict()      // same
dict([[1, "x"], [2.5, "y"]])     // => dict({"1": "x", "2.5": "y"}) — keys stringified
dict([[1, 2, 3]])                // Error: conversion — an entry is exactly [key, value]

doc.markdown:
The reverse edge is [`d.array()`](kavun:type/dict/array), which answers the
entries key-sorted — the two round-trip up to ordering.

### From a record

doc.code:
dict({a: 1})          // independent dict with the record's entries
dict_view({a: 1})     // a dict sharing the record's map — see record: views

doc.markdown:
The `_view` pair is the one place the constructor rule does **not** apply: `dict()` / `record()` always build
a new value, and `dict_view()` / `record_view()` always share storage — that is their entire job, and the only
way to get shared storage in the language. On an argument that is already the target type there is nothing to
borrow — `d` already owns its map — so `dict_view(d)` answers `d` itself and `is_view(d)` stays `false`.

## Keys and the index operator

Keys are strings. A non-string key stores under (and looks up by) its **canonical text** — the same reading
`.string()` answers: `d[65]` keys `"65"`, `d[b'A']` keys `"A"`, `d[true]` keys `"true"`, and a high octet like
`b'\xFF'` keys its escape text `"\xff"`. A value with no canonical text — a `dict`, a `record`, a callable,
`undefined` — raises `invalid_index_type`, never silently keys by its rendering. A sequence-typed key (`array`,
`range`) raises too: a transcode is not a key.

doc.code:
d = dict({a: 1})
d[1] = "x"            // stored under "1"
d[1.5] = "y"          // stored under "1.5"
d[true] = "z"         // stored under "true"
d[b'A'] = "w"         // stored under "A" — a byte's canonical text is its ASCII symbol
d[b'\xFF'] = "v"      // stored under "\xff" — a high octet's text is its escape
d["1"]                // => "x" — the same entry d[1] wrote

d[{k: 1}]             // Error: invalid_index_type — record has no string conversion
d[dict()]             // Error: invalid_index_type
d[func() { return 1 }]  // Error: invalid_index_type
d[undefined]          // Error: invalid_index_type
d[b'\xFF']            // => "v" — the same entry d[b'\xFF'] wrote, under "\xff"
d[[1, 2]]             // Error: invalid_index_type — a sequence is not a key
d[range(1, 3)]        // Error: invalid_index_type

doc.markdown:
Reading a missing key answers `undefined` — presence and "attached `undefined`" are told apart with
`contains`:

doc.code:
d = dict({a: 1})
d["nope"]             // => undefined
d.contains("nope")    // => false

doc.markdown: `d[k] = v` is a statement, not an expression. On a frozen dict it raises `not_assignable`:

doc.code:
f = dict({a: 1}).freeze()
f["b"] = 2            // Error: not_assignable

doc.markdown:
Dot access on a dict is **not** element access — that namespace belongs to member functions, and it is refused
in **both directions**: `d.a` (read) and `d.a = 5` (write) each raise `invalid_selector`
(`type dict has no property a`). In a chain the refusal hits at the first dot — `d.x.y = 1` raises at `.x`.
Element access is always `d["a"]` / `d["a"] = 5`; the selector grammar is [`record`](kavun:type/record)'s
feature.

## Operators

| operator | meaning | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `d1 + d2` | merge, last (right) wins on key collision | `dict` |
| `dict + record`, `record + dict` | merge — either operand being a `dict` makes the result a `dict` | `dict` |
| `d - "key"` | new dict without that entry; missing key is a no-op; non-mutating | `dict` |
| `k in d` | key membership, with `contains`' rules (below) | `bool` |
| `==` / `!=` | deep structural equality; crosses `dict`/`record` freely | `bool` |
| `< > <= >=` | **not defined** — a map has no total order | raises |

doc.code:
dict({a: 1, b: 2}) + dict({b: 9, c: 3})   // => dict({"a": 1, "b": 9, "c": 3})
dict({a: 1}) + {b: 2}                     // => dict({"a": 1, "b": 2})
{a: 1} + dict({b: 2})                     // => dict({"a": 1, "b": 2})

dict({a: 1, b: 2}) - "a"                  // => dict({"b": 2}) — the receiver is untouched
dict({a: 1}) - "zz"                       // => dict({"a": 1}) — missing key, no-op

doc.markdown:
`-` takes a `string` key only; there is no reflected form (`"key" - d` is not defined).

`in` asks key membership and follows `contains`' acceptance — it converts what a key probe converts and raises
on everything else, never answering a silent `false` for an operand it cannot read:

doc.code:
"a" in dict({a: 1})               // => true
"z" in dict({a: 1})               // => false
1 in dict([["1", 5]])             // => true — the int converts to the key "1"

dict({a: 1}) in dict({a: 1, b: 2})     // Error: not_implemented — the submap reading is reserved
(func() { return 1 }) in dict({a: 1})  // Error: invalid_value — an operator operand is always a value;
                                       // the predicate reading is contains(f)/any(f)
undefined in dict({a: 1})              // Error: invalid_argument_type — not convertible to a key

doc.markdown:
Equality is deep — element values compare by their own equality, key order never matters, and `dict` and
`record` compare across each other:

doc.code:
dict({a: [1, 2]}) == dict({a: [1, 2]})   // => true
dict({a: [1, 2]}) == dict({a: [1, 3]})   // => false
dict({a: 1}) == {a: 1}                   // => true — dict/record cross freely

doc.markdown:
## Iteration

A map's element is its key, so the single-variable form yields **keys**; the two-variable form yields
`(key, value)`; values alone are spelled with the blank:

doc.code:
d = dict({b: 2, a: 1})
for k in d {}             // k: "a", "b" — the keys
for k, v in d {}          // ("a", 1), ("b", 2)
for _, v in d {}          // 1, 2 — the values spelling

doc.markdown:
**Key order is lexical, everywhere.** Iteration, every member that visits keys (`for_each`, `reduce`, `index`,
`map`, `keep`, `count`, `any`, `all`, …), `keys()`/`values()`, the `array()` entries, and rendering and
encoding all walk the same single order, so a map-driven program answers the same thing on every run — a
display, a `json.encode` payload and a binary blob included. Keys are strings and sort as strings do
(byte-wise: `"10"` before `"2"`, uppercase before lowercase).

doc.code:
d = dict({zebra: 1, apple: 2, mango: 3})
d.keys()                       // => ["apple", "mango", "zebra"]
for k in d {}                 // "apple", "mango", "zebra" — the same order
array(d)                       // => [["apple", 2], ["mango", 3], ["zebra", 1]]

doc.markdown:
Order is a *contract*, not an insertion memory: a dict has no insertion order to preserve, and re-inserting a
key does not move it. It is also not a sortable sequence.

## Callbacks

A member that takes a function — the predicate reading of the search members, `map`, `for_each`, `reduce` — calls it
in the **fewest form it accepts**, read from the callable's arity and whether it is variadic, never from what kind of
callable it is:

- a per-element callback gets the key when it accepts one argument, else `(key, value)`; anything else raises;
- a `reduce` callback gets `(acc, key)` when it accepts two arguments, else `(acc, key, value)`; anything else
raises.

So `func(x, ...rest)` and `func(...args)` get the key, and a builtin or a bound member is a callback like any other
(`min` and `"abc".contains` accept one argument). A lambda is the one way to call a callable in another form — choose
the form, reorder, fix or drop arguments:

doc.code:
d = dict({a: 1, b: 2})
d.keep(func(k, v) { return v > 1 })                   // => dict({"b": 2}) — accepts two, not one
d.count(func(k, ...rest) { return k == "a" })         // => 1 — accepts one: the key
d.keep(["b", "c"].contains)                           // => dict({"b": 2})
d.reduce(0, func(acc, k, v) { return acc + v })       // => 3

members.name: all
members.summary: Report whether every entry matches a key, a set of keys or a predicate; see [`any`](kavun:type/dict/any).

doc.markdown: A function argument gets the key, or `(key, value)` when it does not accept one argument ([callbacks](kavun:type/dict#callbacks)).

members.name: any
members.summary: Report whether some entry matches a key, a set of keys or a predicate.

doc.markdown: A function argument gets the key, or `(key, value)` when it does not accept one argument ([callbacks](kavun:type/dict#callbacks)).

doc.code:
d = dict({a: 1, b: 2})
d.any("a")                                   // => true
d.all(func(k, v) { return v > 0 })           // => true

members.name: array
members.summary: Answer the entries as a new array of `[key, value]` pairs, key-sorted.

doc.markdown:
`d.array()` materialises the entries, key-sorted — each entry exactly a 2-element `[key, value]` array. It is
the inverse of the entries constructor, so the two round-trip up to ordering:

members.name: contains
members.summary: Report whether some key matches a key, a member of a set of keys or a predicate.

doc.markdown:
All of the search members match **keys** — the value axis is `d.values()`'s job. They share three readings: a
single value (converted to a key the way the index operator converts), a variadic set of them ("∈ the set"), or a
predicate (it gets the key, or `(key, value)` when it does not accept one argument — [callbacks](kavun:type/dict#callbacks)). No
argument raises; mixing a function into a set raises:

doc.code:
d = dict({a: 1, b: 2})
d.contains("a")                              // => true
d.contains(1)                                // => false — the key "1" is absent (never matches values)
d.contains("x", "a")                         // => true — any of the set
d.contains(func(k) { return k.len() > 1 })   // => false
d.contains()                                 // Error: wrong_num_arguments
d.contains(dict({a: 1}))                     // Error: not_implemented — the submap reading is reserved

members.name: copy
members.summary: Answer an independent deep copy.

doc.code:
d = dict({a: [1, 2]})
c = d.copy()                   // deep: c["a"] is an independent array

members.name: copy_shallow
members.summary: Answer a copy with a fresh top level, nested values still shared.

doc.code:
d = dict({a: [1, 2]})
s = d.copy_shallow()           // one level: s is a new map, s["a"] is d's array

members.name: count
members.summary: Count the keys that match a key, a set of keys or a predicate.

doc.markdown: A function argument gets the key, or `(key, value)` when it does not accept one argument ([callbacks](kavun:type/dict#callbacks)).

doc.code:
d = dict({a: 1, b: 2})
d.count("a", "b", "z")                       // => 2
d.count(func(k, v) { return v > 1 })         // => 1

members.name: date
members.summary: Build a `date` from the named components `year`, `month` and `day`; an unknown key raises; see [`time`](kavun:type/dict/time).

members.name: dict
members.summary: Answer a new, independent, mutable **shallow** copy, exactly `dict(d)` / `d.copy_shallow()`.

doc.markdown:
`d.dict()` converts from a dict to a dict, and like every conversion it **constructs**: an independent
`dict` with the same entries, exactly `dict(d)` / `d.copy_shallow()`. It is equal to the receiver but is not
the receiver, so a write through it never reaches `d`. Shared storage is `record_view()`'s job, never a
conversion's:

doc.code:
d = dict({a: 1})
e = d.dict()
e == d                 // => true — equal entries
e["b"] = 2
d                      // => dict({"a": 1}) — untouched

members.name: for_each
members.summary: Call the callback on every entry, in sorted key order — always a **full pass**, its return value ignored — and return the receiver.

doc.markdown:
The callback gets the key, or `(key, value)` when it does not accept one argument ([callbacks](kavun:type/dict#callbacks)).

`for_each(fn)` makes one full pass in sorted key order — the callback's return value is ignored (early exit is
`break`'s job, in a `for` loop) — and returns the receiver. Being the side-effecting member, its order is the
most visible of all: a `for_each` that prints or accumulates gives the same result on every run.

doc.code:
d = dict({a: 1})
d.for_each(func(k, v) {})         // visits every entry, keys ascending; answers d itself

o = []
dict({zebra: 1, apple: 2}).for_each(func(k) { o.append_in_place(k) })
o                                  // => ["apple", "zebra"]

members.name: format
members.summary: Render the value per the [format mini-language](kavun:doc/format_mini_language).

doc.code: dict({a: 1}).format()          // the render: dict({"a": 1})

members.name: freeze
members.summary: Answer a deep-immutable *copy*; the source and its aliases are untouched.

doc.code:
f = dict({a: [1]}).freeze()    // deep: the dict and its elements are immutable
f["a"].push_in_place(2)        // Error: not_mutable — the inner array froze too

members.name: freeze_shallow
members.summary: Mark the header you hold immutable without detaching; reassign to see it (`d = d.freeze_shallow()`).

doc.code:
g = dict({a: [1]}).freeze_shallow()
g["b"] = 2                     // Error: not_assignable — the map itself is frozen
g["a"].push_in_place(2)        // fine — one level only, the inner array stayed mutable

members.name: index
members.summary: Answer the first key, in sorted order, that matches a key or a predicate, or `undefined` (the default when given) on a miss.

doc.markdown:
A function argument gets the key, or `(key, value)` when it does not accept one argument ([callbacks](kavun:type/dict#callbacks)).

`index(x[, default])` answers a **key** — the map's locator is its element, not a position. It visits keys in
sorted order, so a predicate's answer is deterministic; a miss answers `undefined`, or the trailing default:

doc.code:
dict({apple: 1, pear: 2}).index(func(k, v) { return v == 2 })   // => "pear"
dict({z: 1, b: 1, a: 1}).index(func(k, v) { return v == 1 })    // => "a" — sorted visit
dict({a: 1}).index("z")                                         // => undefined
dict({a: 1}).index("z", "fallback")                             // => "fallback"

doc.markdown: There is no `index_last` — with no defined order, "last" does not exist on a dict.

members.name: is_empty
members.summary: Report whether the dict has no entries.

doc.code:
d = dict({b: 2, a: 1, c: 3})
d.is_empty()     // => false

members.name: is_true
members.summary: Report truthiness, which is non-emptiness: `!!x` ⟺ `x != dict()`.

doc.code:
dict({a: 1}).is_true()         // => true — a dict is truthy iff non-empty
dict().is_true()               // => false
!!dict()                       // => false — same test

members.name: keep
members.summary: Keep only the entries whose key is in the key set, or which match a predicate; see [`remove`](kavun:type/dict/remove).

doc.markdown: A function argument gets the key, or `(key, value)` when it does not accept one argument ([callbacks](kavun:type/dict#callbacks)).

members.name: keep_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `keep`.

members.name: keys
members.summary: Answer the keys as a new array, sorted.

doc.code:
d = dict({b: 2, a: 1, c: 3})
d.keys()         // => ["a", "b", "c"] — a fresh array, sorted

doc.markdown:
`keys()`/`values()` answer new arrays; mutating them does not touch the dict. They are also the spelling for
every value-axis or whole-collection question the dict deliberately does not answer itself:

doc.code:
dict({a: 1, b: 2}).values().sum()        // => 3
dict({z: 1, a: 2}).keys().min()          // => "a"
dict({a: 1}).values().contains(1)        // => true — "does any entry hold this value?"

members.name: len
members.summary: Answer the number of entries.

members.name: map
members.summary: Answer a new dict with the same keys, each value replaced by the callback's result.

doc.markdown:
`map` transforms the **attachment** with the keys fixed: the callback's result becomes the new value for that key,
and the answer is a new `dict` of the same keys. The callback gets the key, or `(key, value)` when it does not accept
one argument ([callbacks](kavun:type/dict#callbacks)); anything else raises. Re-keying is a different operation — and one that can
collide — so `map` never touches the key axis (build a new dict via `reduce` or a loop if you need it):

doc.code:
dict({a: 1, b: 2}).map(func(k, v) { return v * 10 })   // => dict({"a": 10, "b": 20})
dict({a: 1, b: 2}).map(func(k) { return k + "!" })     // => dict({"a": "a!", "b": "b!"})

doc.markdown: There is no `map_in_place` — `map`'s result is a new dict by contract.

members.name: merge
members.summary: Merge the entries of the `dict` and `record` arguments into a new dict, in argument order, last one winning.

doc.markdown:
`merge` is the whole add side. It is variadic over `dict` **and** `record` arguments; entries are applied in
argument order, last one wins; no arguments is a no-op; any non-map argument raises `invalid_argument_type`:

doc.code:
dict({a: 1}).merge(dict({b: 2}), {a: 9})       // => dict({"a": 9, "b": 2})
dict({a: 1}).merge(dict({a: 2}), dict({a: 3})) // => dict({"a": 3}) — argument order, last wins
dict({a: 1}).merge()                           // => dict({"a": 1})
dict({a: 1}).merge([1, 2])                     // Error: invalid_argument_type — dict or record only

m = dict({a: 1})
m.merge_in_place(dict({b: 2}))     // returns m itself; m is now dict({"a": 1, "b": 2})
dict({a: 1}).freeze().merge_in_place(dict({b: 2}))   // Error: not_mutable

doc.markdown: There is deliberately **no single-entry add member** (`set`, `put`, …). The two spellings are:

doc.code:
d := dict()
k := "a"
v := 1
d[k] = v                     // the mutating statement
d.merge(dict([[k, v]]))      // non-mutating, via the entries constructor

members.name: merge_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `merge`.

members.name: range
members.summary: Build a `range` from the named components `start`, `stop` and `step`; an unknown key raises; see [`time`](kavun:type/dict/time).

members.name: record
members.summary: Answer an independent record with the same entries.

doc.markdown:
`d.record()` answers an independent record with the same entries; `d.record_view()` answers a record **sharing
the dict's map** — the performance opt-in when you want record-style field access over live dict data:

doc.code:
d = dict({a: 1})
r = d.record_view()
d["b"] = 2
r.b                    // => 2 — the view sees the write

doc.markdown:
The `default` is taken for interface uniformity — every conversion carries it — and is never used: the
conversion is total.

members.name: record_view
members.summary: Answer a record sharing the dict's map; see [`record`](kavun:type/dict/record).

members.name: reduce
members.summary: Fold the entries, in sorted key order, into an accumulator that starts at `init`.

doc.markdown:
`reduce(init, fn)` folds over the entries in **sorted key order** (deterministic by construction). The callback
gets `(acc, key)`, or `(acc, key, value)` when it does not accept two arguments ([callbacks](kavun:type/dict#callbacks)):

doc.code:
dict({b: 1, a: 1}).reduce("", func(acc, k) { return acc + k })              // => "ab"
dict({b: 2, a: 1, c: 3}).reduce(0, func(acc, k, v) { return acc*10 + v })   // => 123

members.name: remove
members.summary: Remove the entries whose key is in the key set, or which match a predicate.

doc.markdown:
Both act on whole entries and take either a **key set** (variadic strings — or values convertible to keys) or a
**predicate**, and the names say which way each one goes: `remove` drops the matching entries, `keep` answers
exactly them. A missing key is a silent no-op. A predicate gets the key, or `(key, value)` when it does not accept
one argument ([callbacks](kavun:type/dict#callbacks)). Neither has a no-argument form — a map's keys are identities, never filler, so there is no
blank set to read against:

doc.code:
dict({a: 1, b: 2}).remove("a")                   // => dict({"b": 2})
dict({a: 1, b: 2, c: 3}).remove("a", "c")        // => dict({"b": 2})
dict({a: 1}).remove("zz")                        // => dict({"a": 1}) — absent, no-op
dict({aa: 1, b: 2}).remove(func(k) { return k.len() > 1 })     // => dict({"b": 2})
dict({a: 1, b: 2}).remove(func(k, v) { return v > 1 })         // => dict({"a": 1})

dict({a: 1, b: 2, c: 3}).keep("a", "c")        // => dict({"a": 1, "c": 3})
dict({a: 1, b: 2}).keep(func(k, v) { return v > 1 })         // => dict({"b": 2})

dict({a: 1}).keep()      // Error: wrong_num_arguments — a map has no blank reading
dict({a: 1}).remove()      // Error: wrong_num_arguments

doc.markdown:
A match set is homogeneous: mixing a function with keys in one call raises. The `_in_place` twins mutate the
receiver and return it; on a frozen dict they raise `not_mutable`.

members.name: remove_in_place
members.summary: In-place twin of `remove`.

members.name: time
members.summary: Build a `time` from the named components; an unknown key raises.

doc.markdown:
`d.time()` and `d.range()` are the component-form constructors: the dict supplies named components, and an
unknown key raises (`invalid_value`) rather than being ignored:

doc.code:
dict({year: 2026, month: 8, day: 29}).time()   // => time("2026-08-29T00:00:00Z")
dict({start: 1, stop: 5}).range()              // => range(1, 5)
dict({start: 1, xx: 5}).range()                // Error: invalid_value — unknown component "xx"

members.name: values
members.summary: Answer the values as a new array, in `keys()` order; see [`keys`](kavun:type/dict/keys).

doc.code:
d = dict({b: 2, a: 1, c: 3})
d.values()       // => [1, 2, 3] — a fresh array, in keys() order

types.name: error
types.summary: A failure as a first-class value.

doc.markdown:
## Overview

An `error` is a value that carries a payload describing a failure. Errors reach a script two ways:

- **constructed** — `error(payload)` wraps any value; the script raises it itself with `raise(...)`;
- **raised by the runtime** — division by zero, a bad index, a failed conversion, … — and caught with
`recover()` inside a deferred function.

Every error is **truthy** — an error without a payload is still an error, and there is no zero error
(`error()` with no arguments is itself a runtime error: `(error) expected (payload[, fatal]), got 0 arguments`).
Each error carries a machine-readable `kind()` tag, a `value()` payload, and a **category** saying where it came
from, read with `is_runtime()` / `is_user()` / `is_requirement()`.

### Categories

Every kind belongs to exactly one category — the error's origin, an axis independent of what went wrong:

| category | predicate | raised by | reaches a script? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| runtime | `is_runtime()` | a builtin, a member function or a stdlib module | yes |
| user | `is_user()` | the script's own `error(...)` / `raise(...)` | yes |
| requirement | `is_requirement()` | the script's own `require(cond, payload)` | yes |
| system | — | the VM itself: stack overflow, an internal invariant, a host defect | **never** |

A system error is always fatal, so it bypasses every `recover()` and only ever reaches the host — which is why
there is no `is_system()` to call. The host reads the category from `RuntimeError.Category` (see
[embedding](kavun:doc/embedding#handling-errors)).

## Construction

doc.code:
error("boom")               // payload "boom", kind "user"
error(42)                   // any payload type
error({code: 404})          // including containers
error(undefined)            // legal: the payload-less error — still truthy
error(error("inner"))       // => error("inner") — an error argument is never re-wrapped
error("boom", true)         // second argument: fatal flag — see below

doc.markdown:
`error(x)` **wraps** its argument — it is a constructor, not a conversion, so there is no `.error()` member
on other types and no conversion *from* `error` back into a payload type.

**An argument that is already an error is answered as-is**, never wrapped a second time: `error(err)` is
`err`. A bare re-wrap only ever added an unlabelled layer, and it relabelled the payload's own diagnosis —
a caught runtime error came back out as kind `"user"` in the user category. The severity form keeps the
payload and kind and changes only the flag, which is exactly what `raise(err, fatal)` already did:

doc.code:
e = error("boom")
error(e) == e               // => true — the same error, not a nested one
error(e).value()            // => "boom" — a string, not an error
error(e, true)              // fatal; kind() and value() are still "user"/"boom"

// a runtime error keeps its own diagnosis through the constructor
c = func() r { defer func() { r = recover() }(); (1).nope() }()   // a caught invalid_method error
error(c).kind()             // => "invalid_method" — not relabelled to "user"
error(c).is_runtime()       // => true — the category travels with the error too

doc.markdown:
Deliberate nesting is spelled with a payload that **names** the cause, which is the annotated chain a bare
re-wrap could never express:

doc.code:
e = error("config file not found")
error({msg: "loading config failed", cause: e})   // the chain, labelled

doc.markdown:
The optional second argument is a `bool` fatal flag. A fatal error is **not catchable**: `raise(error("x",
true))` unwinds past every `recover()` and terminates the script. Use it for states no handler should paper
over.

## Raising and catching

`raise(x)` raises. A non-error argument is wrapped first — `raise("text")` and `raise(42)` raise a kind
`"user"` error with that payload. `recover()`, called inside a deferred function, answers the in-flight error
and stops the unwinding; with nothing in flight it answers `undefined`.

Note the **named result** (`res`): a plain local assigned inside the deferred function would be lost — the
named result is how a handler substitutes a value. In a script's own body, which has no named result, a
top-level `defer` assigns a variable instead (see [`defer` at the top
level](kavun:doc/language#defer-at-the-top-level-of-a-script)).

### `require(cond, payload)`

The input check a script opens with. When `cond` is true it answers `undefined` and the script carries on;
otherwise it raises a recoverable error of kind `requirement` carrying `payload` **untouched** — so a
structured rejection reaches the host as structure, not as a sentence.

doc.code:
input := {amount: 5d}                 // the host's binding
require(is_decimal(input.amount), {field: "amount", reason: "not a number"})
require(input.amount > 0d,        {field: "amount", reason: "must be positive"})
// the happy path follows

doc.markdown:
Truthiness is the same `is_true()` uses. Exactly two arguments; anything else is `wrong_num_arguments`.

### Selective re-raise

Handle the kinds you expect; re-raise everything else unchanged (`raise(e)` keeps the original kind and
payload):

A `division_by_zero` handled this way answers the substitute; an `index_out_of_bounds` raised in the same
position passes through to the outer handler with its kind intact.

## Operators

Errors **propagate by raising**: an error is not a number, a string, or a flag, so combining it with anything
raises `invalid_binary_operator` — whichever side it stands on. Only equality is defined, and it compares
**payloads** (the kind and flags do not participate):

doc.code:
error("boom") == error("boom")   // => true — equal payloads
error("boom") == error("bam")    // => false
error(1) == error(1)             // => true
error(1) == 1                    // => false — an error never equals a non-error
error("a") != error("b")         // => true

error("x") + 1                   // Error: invalid_binary_operator: error + int
1 + error("x")                   // Error: invalid_binary_operator: int + error
error("x") + error("y")          // Error: invalid_binary_operator: error + error
error(1) < error(2)              // Error: invalid_binary_operator — no ordering
!error("x")                      // => false — every error is truthy

doc.markdown:
## Every error kind

Each kind has one severity and one [category](kavun:type/error#categories), always. **Recoverable** kinds can reach a script's
`recover()`; **system** kinds are fatal and only ever reach the host.

### Script and script-data kinds — recoverable, category *runtime*

| kind | raised by | example trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `division_by_zero` | `/` or `%` by zero, on `int` and `decimal` | `1 / 0`, `1d / 0d` |
| `invalid_argument_type` | an argument outside a member's accepted readings | `[1, 2].join(1.5)` |
| `invalid_value` | a value of the right type outside the valid domain — overflow, a declared limit, an empty sequence | `range(1, 4, 0)`; `"ab".repeat(1e12)`; `[].first()` |
| `wrong_num_arguments` | wrong argument count | `"a".upper(1)`, `[1, 2].chunk()` |
| `index_out_of_bounds` | index outside the sequence | `[1, 2][5]` |
| `invalid_index_type` | index of the wrong type | `[1, 2]["a"]` |
| `invalid_selector` | a selector a type does not answer | `{a: 1}.b.c` |
| `invalid_unpack_type` | destructuring a value that cannot be unpacked | `a, b := 5` |
| `not_mutable` | any mutating member on a frozen receiver | `freeze([1, 2]).push_in_place(3)` |
| `not_assignable` | an assignment statement into a frozen container | `a := freeze([1, 2]); a[0] = 9` |
| `not_accessible` / `not_appendable` / `not_deletable` / `not_iterable` / `not_sliceable` | an operation the type does not support | `range(1, 10)[1:3]` |
| `invalid_method` | calling a member the type does not have | `(5).len()` |
| `invalid_binary_operator` / `invalid_unary_operator` | an operator pair with no meaning | `error("x") + 1`; `-[1]` |
| `not_callable` | calling a non-callable value | `x := 5; x()` |
| `not_implemented` | a reading deferred to a type that does not exist yet | `range(1, 5).contains(1..3)` |
| `conversion` | a failed conversion or parse | `"abc".int()`, `decimal("abc")`, `(1e39).decimal()` |
| `unsupported_format_spec` | a malformed or unsupported format spec | `(5).format("{:,}")`, `format("{0:", [1])` |
| `formatting` | a value that cannot be rendered at all | — |
| `undefined_variable` | reading a name the runtime cannot resolve | — |
| `module_not_found` | `import` of a name that is not registered | `import("nope")` |
| `module_not_allowed` | bytecode importing a builtin module the host did not grant (checked by the VM before the first instruction; never reaches `recover()`) | `import("os")` without a grant |
| `json_encoding` | a value with no JSON representation | `json.encode(func(){})` |
| `json_decoding` | malformed JSON input | `json.decode("{")` |
| `binary_encoding` | a value that cannot be binary-encoded, or corrupt input | — |
| `io` | the world refused: a file, a directory, an environment variable, a process | `fs.remove("/nope")` |

### Script-authored kinds — recoverable

| kind | category | raised by | example trigger |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `user` | user | `error(...)` construction, `raise(x)` | `raise("text")`, `raise({code: 42})` |
| `requirement` | requirement | `require(cond, payload)` with a falsy condition | `require(false, "bad input")` |

### System kinds — **fatal**, category *system*

These bypass every `recover()`, skip every remaining `defer`, and reach the host only. A script can never hold
one, which is why no `is_system()` predicate exists.

| kind | means |
| --- | --- |
| `stack_overflow` | the call-frame or operand stack ran out — usually unbounded recursion |
| `internal` | a VM invariant was violated, or a Go panic was contained at the run boundary |
| `host` | a host setup mistake: `SetValueType` on a builtin slot, an unregistered module ID |

`not_mutable` is uniform: **every** mutating member on an immutable receiver raises it, whatever the verb —
and before it looks at its arguments, so `[1].freeze().sort_in_place(1)` raises `not_mutable`, not
`wrong_num_arguments`.
`not_assignable` is the assignment statement's own kind.

## Telling apart the kinds of wrong

A kind says what failed, not **whose fault it was** — and it cannot: `int(x)` does not know where `x` came
from. Three kinds carry that signal:

| signal | read it as |
| --- | --- |
| `requirement` | the script's own input check rejected the caller's data. The payload says which field and why. |
| `conversion`, `json_decoding`, `io` | the data or the world did not cooperate — a bad parse, malformed input, a missing file |
| anything else | most likely a defect in the script itself |

A host that wants to distinguish "the caller sent bad data" from "the rules have a bug" should branch on that,
not on the message text. See [embedding](kavun:doc/embedding#handling-errors).

members.name: array
members.summary: Answer a new one-element `array` holding the receiver.

doc.markdown: Total, so the default is never used.

doc.code: error(1).array()    // => [error(1)]

members.name: bool
members.summary: Answer `true`: every error is truthy, whatever its payload.

doc.markdown:
Both answer `true` for every error — truthiness is the single stated base case: an error is always truthy,
payload or no payload. `bool()` does **not** parse the payload.

doc.code:
error(0).is_true()        // => true
error(0).bool()           // => true
error("false").bool()     // => true — not a payload parse
error(undefined).is_true() // => true

doc.markdown:
The `default` is taken for interface uniformity — every conversion carries it — and is never used: the
conversion is total.

members.name: copy
members.summary: Answer an error with a deep copy of the payload.

doc.markdown:
Real deep operations on the payload — not header no-ops. `copy()` answers an error with a deep copy of the
payload; `freeze()` answers an error whose payload is deep-frozen (the receiver is unchanged).

doc.code:
e := error([1, 2])
c := e.copy()
c.value().push_in_place(3)
format(c.value())              // => "[1, 2, 3]"
format(e.value())              // => "[1, 2]" — the original payload untouched

fe := e.freeze()
is_immutable(fe.value())       // => true
is_immutable(e.value())        // => false

members.name: format
members.summary: Render the value per the [format mini-language](kavun:doc/format_mini_language).

doc.markdown:
The universal render. The default form renders the payload — whatever its type, exactly as `string()` does;
`"v"` shows the constructor form. An f-string, `format(...)` and `json.encode` all go through this render, so
`json.encode(e)` is `{"error": <the default render>}`, the render encoded exactly as a `string` is — escaped, and
raising `json_encoding` when it holds octets that are not symbols.

doc.code:
error("boom").format()      // => "boom"
error([1, 2]).format()      // => "[1, 2]" — a non-string payload renders as its string form
error("boom").format("v")   // => "error(\"boom\")"

members.name: freeze
members.summary: Answer an error whose payload is deep-frozen, leaving the receiver unchanged; see [`copy`](kavun:type/error/copy).

members.name: is_requirement
members.summary: Report whether the script raised the error with `require(cond, payload)`; see [`is_runtime`](kavun:type/error/is_runtime).

members.name: is_runtime
members.summary: Report whether the runtime raised the error — a builtin, a member function or a stdlib module.

doc.markdown:
The [category](kavun:type/error#categories) predicates — where the error came from. Exactly one is `true` for any error a
script can hold.

doc.code:
error("boom").is_user()            // => true
error("boom").is_runtime()         // => false
error("boom").is_requirement()     // => false

zero := 0
e := func() r { defer func() { r = recover() }(); 1 / zero }()   // a recovered 1/0 error
e.kind()                            // => "division_by_zero"
e.is_runtime()                      // => true

e = func() r { defer func() { r = recover() }(); require(false, {field: "amount"}) }()   // a recovered require
e.kind()                            // => "requirement"
e.is_requirement()                  // => true
e.value()                           // => {"field": "amount"} — the payload, untouched

doc.markdown:
There is no `is_system()`: a system error is always fatal and never reaches a script. There is no `is_fatal()`
either — the fatal flag's only reader is the host (`RuntimeError.Fatal`). A script *sets* it, with
`error(x, true)` or `raise(x, true)`, and can never read it back off a caught error, because a caught error
is recoverable by construction.

members.name: is_true
members.summary: Report truthiness, which is always `true` for an error; see [`bool`](kavun:type/error/bool).

members.name: is_user
members.summary: Report whether the script built the error with `error(...)` / `raise(...)`; see [`is_runtime`](kavun:type/error/is_runtime).

members.name: kind
members.summary: Answer the machine-readable tag, a `string`.

doc.markdown:
The machine-readable tag, a `string`. Constructed and `raise`d errors are `"user"`; runtime errors carry the
tags in the [kind table](kavun:type/error#every-error-kind) below. This is the value a handler matches on.

doc.code:
error("boom").kind()          // => "user"
error("boom", true).kind()    // => "user" — the fatal flag is not a kind

members.name: runes
members.summary: Render the payload as `runes`; see [`string`](kavun:type/error/string).

doc.markdown: As for [`string`](kavun:type/error/string), the `default` is answered only when the payload has no rendering.

members.name: string
members.summary: Render the payload as a `string`, the same path `format()` uses.

doc.markdown:
The **payload's** render — the same path `format()` uses — as `string`/`runes`. This is a render of the
content, not a laundering conversion: the result describes the payload, whatever its type. The free
`string(e)` matches.

doc.code:
error("boom").string()   // => "boom"
error(42).string()       // => "42"
error("boom").runes()    // => u"boom"
string(error(42))        // => "42"

doc.markdown:
A payload with no rendering (a host value without a `format`) raises, or answers the `default` when one is
given.

members.name: value
members.summary: Answer the payload, exactly as wrapped.

doc.markdown:
The payload, exactly as wrapped — and the ONLY structured channel an error has. `kind()` is a tag; there is no
further field set on a runtime error.

| the error came from | `value()` is |
| --- | --- |
| the runtime (a builtin, member, module) | the message `string`, always non-empty: `1/0`'s is `"division by zero"` |
| `error(x)` / `raise(x)` | `x`, untouched — any type |
| `require(cond, x)` | `x`, untouched — any type |

doc.code:
error(42).value()          // => 42
error(undefined).value()   // => undefined

doc.markdown: So a script that wants to hand a structured rejection to its host raises one:

types.name: exec.command
types.summary: A prepared external command, as `exec.exec(name, args...)` answers it.

doc.markdown:
## Overview

`exec.command` is owned by the [`exec`](kavun:module/exec) module. Configure it (`set_dir`, `set_env`, `set_path`),
then run it once — `run()`, `output()`, `combined_output()`, or `start()` followed by `wait()`. A refusal or a failed
run raises `io` naming the member. It renders as `<exec.command:NAME>`; no `string()`.

doc.code:
exec := import("exec")
string(exec.exec("echo", "hi").output())   // => "hi\n" — output() answers bytes
c := exec.exec("sh", "-c", "exit 3")
c.start()
c.process().wait().success            // => false

doc.markdown:
## Operators

| operator | reading |
| --- | --- |
| `==` / `!=` | the same command (identity) |
| `!` | a command is always truthy |
| everything else | raises |

members.name: array
members.summary: Answer a new one-element `array` holding the receiver.

doc.markdown: Total, so the default is never used.

doc.code: import("exec").exec("echo").array().len()   // => 1 — building a command runs nothing

members.name: combined_output
members.summary: Run the command and answer its stdout and stderr together, as `bytes`; see [`output`](kavun:type/exec.command/output).

members.summary: Answer the command itself.

members.name: format
members.summary: Render the command per the [format mini-language](kavun:doc/format_mini_language).

members.name: freeze
members.summary: Answer the command itself; see [`copy`](kavun:type/exec.command/copy).

members.name: is_true
members.summary: Report truthiness: a command is always truthy.

members.name: output
members.summary: Run the command and answer its stdout, as `bytes`.

members.name: process
members.summary: Answer the started command's [`exec.process`](kavun:type/exec.process); before `start()` it raises `invalid_value`.

members.name: run
members.summary: Run the command and wait for it; raises `io` if it cannot start or ends with a failure status.

members.name: set_dir
members.summary: Set the working directory; configure before running.

members.name: set_env
members.summary: Set the environment, an array of `"K=V"` strings; configure before running.

members.name: set_path
members.summary: Set the program path; configure before running.

members.summary: Start the command without waiting for it.

members.summary: Wait for a started command to end; see [`start`](kavun:type/exec.command/start).

types.name: exec.process
types.summary: A process, as `exec.start_process`, `exec.find_process` and `command.process()` answer it.

doc.markdown:
## Overview

`exec.process` is owned by the [`exec`](kavun:module/exec) module. Every member reaches the operating system; a
refusal raises `io` naming the member. It renders as `<exec.process:PID>`; no `string()`.

doc.code:
exec := import("exec")
p := exec.start_process("/bin/sleep", ["sleep", "0"], "", [])
p.pid() > 0                // => true
st := p.wait()             // {pid: …, exited: true, success: true, status: "exit status 0"}
st.success                 // => true

doc.markdown:
## Operators

| operator | reading |
| --- | --- |
| `==` / `!=` | the same process (by pid) |
| `!` | a process is always truthy |
| everything else | raises |

members.summary: Answer a new one-element `array` holding the receiver.

doc.markdown: Total, so the default is never used.

doc.code:
c := import("exec").exec("echo")
c.start()
c.process().array().len()   // => 1
c.wait()

members.summary: Kill the process.

members.summary: Answer the process id.

members.summary: Release the resources held for the process.

members.summary: Send the signal `sig` to the process.

types.name: fin.year_fraction
types.summary: A length of time **in years**, as an exact ratio.

doc.markdown:
## Overview

A year fraction is the days a day-count convention counts over the year length it takes. It is the `f` the interest
functions take, kept exact so an accrual never rounds the period before it multiplies. The type is named after its
constructor (`type_name(f)` is `"fin.year_fraction"`) because it exists only for this module. It is owned by the
[`fin`](kavun:module/fin) module.

doc.code:
fin := import("fin")
f := fin.year_fraction_between(d"2026-01-01", d"2026-02-01", "ACT/365F")   // => fin.year_fraction(31, 365)
fin.year_fraction_between(d"2026-02-01", d"2026-03-01", "30E/360")        // => fin.year_fraction(30, 360) — every month is 30 days
fin.year_fraction_between(d"2027-07-01", d"2028-07-01", "ACT/ACT")        // => fin.year_fraction(184, 365, 182, 366) — split at the year end
fin.year_fraction(31, 365)                 // stated directly: 31 counted days over a 365-day year
fin.year_fraction()                        // => fin.year_fraction(0, 1) — the default; falsy
fin.accrue_simple(10000, 0.05d, f, 2, "half_even")   // => 42.47d — interest for January

doc.markdown:
`fin.year_fraction(n1, d1[, n2, d2])` takes `int`s: numerators within `int32`, any sign; denominators **1…65535**
(fin128's own output stays within that, so every value can be rebuilt from its terms). A sum or scale that would
leave those bounds raises `invalid_value`. JSON is the terms array, `[184, 365, 182, 366]`; `json.decode` gives
an array back, which `fin.year_fraction(v...)` rebuilds.

## Operators

| operator | result |
| --- | --- |
| `f + g` | the exact sum |
| `f * n`, `n * f` (`n` an `int`) | scaled — e.g. a year fraction as compounding periods |
| `f < g` (`<=` `>` `>=`), `f == g` | exact, numeric: `fin.year_fraction(31, 365) == fin.year_fraction(62, 730)` |
| `f - g`, `f / n`, `f * f`, `f ± decimal`, `f < 1` | raise — use `f.round(n, mode)` to leave the type |

members.summary: Answer a new one-element `array` holding the receiver.

doc.markdown: Total, so the default is never used.

members.summary: Answer the year fraction itself — it is immutable.

members.summary: Render the year fraction per the [format mini-language](kavun:doc/format_mini_language).

members.name: freeze
members.summary: Answer the year fraction itself; see [`copy`](kavun:type/fin.year_fraction/copy).

members.summary: Report whether the fraction is negative — a period running backwards; see [`is_zero`](kavun:type/fin.year_fraction/is_zero).

members.name: is_positive
members.summary: Report whether the fraction is positive; see [`is_zero`](kavun:type/fin.year_fraction/is_zero).

members.name: is_true
members.summary: Report truthiness: `0/1` is falsy, every other fraction truthy.

members.name: is_zero
members.summary: Report whether the fraction is zero.

members.name: round
members.summary: Answer the decimal reading rounded to `n` fractional places — the only bridge to `decimal`.

doc.markdown:
Rounding is how a value leaves an exact type: the result is a `decimal`, since the fraction cannot hold a rounded
value.

members.summary: Answer the terms as `runes`; see [`string`](kavun:type/fin.year_fraction/string).

doc.code: import("fin").year_fraction(1, 2).runes()   // => u"1/2"

members.name: string
members.summary: Answer the terms as text: `"31/365"`, `"184/365+182/366"` — also what `f"{f}"` renders.

members.summary: Answer `[n1, d1]` or `[n1, d1, n2, d2]`; `fin.year_fraction(f.terms()...) == f` always holds.

types.name: float
types.summary: IEEE 754 double-precision floats with an arithmetic quarantine: no arithmetic result is ever NaN or ±Inf — it raises instead.

doc.markdown:
## Overview

`float` is a 64-bit IEEE 754 binary float. Kavun quarantines its error states: an arithmetic operation whose
result would be NaN or ±Inf **raises a catchable error** instead of letting the sentinel flow through a
calculation silently. The sentinel *values* themselves remain first-class: they can arrive from parses
(`float("inf")`), from the host, or from JSON, and they can be stored, compared, and sorted — only arithmetic
refuses them. `is_nan()` / `is_inf()` interrogate them without triggering the raise being avoided.

`float` belongs to the numeric family alongside [`int`](kavun:type/int) and [`decimal`](kavun:type/decimal). Use `float` for
measurements and physics-style computation where binary rounding is acceptable; use `decimal` for money and any
result that must be exact in base 10 (`0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is `false` on floats and `true` on decimals).

A numeric operation is a `float` member exactly when [`decimal`](kavun:type/decimal) has it — same name, same reading
(pinned by a parity test). Like the operators, no member produces NaN or ±Inf: such a result **raises**
`invalid_value` naming the member.

The rest of float math — trigonometry, `cbrt`, `hypot`, the special functions — is in the
[`math`](kavun:module/math)
module.

## Literals

doc.code:
x = 1.5          // decimal point
k = 1e3          // exponent, 1000.0
m = 2.5e-3       // => 0.0025
n = 3f           // f suffix: a float-typed 3
u = 1_000.25     // underscores group digits
h = 0x1.8p1      // hex float with binary exponent, 3.0

doc.markdown:
## Rendering

`string()` and the default `format()` render the shortest decimal string that round-trips — which is why binary
rounding is visible in full rather than hidden:

The **display** form — what a container shows, and what a doc example writes — always carries a decimal point,
so a whole float never reads back as an `int`:

doc.code:
format("{0}", [[3.0, 3]])   // => "[3.0, 3]" — the float keeps its point, the int has none
format("{0}", [[0.0]])      // => "[0.0]"

doc.markdown:
The **conversion** stays bare on purpose: `3 == 3.0` is `true`, so the two must produce the same key text and
the same `join` output. `(3.0).string()` is `"3"`, `f"{3.0}"` is `"3"`, and `json.encode` is unchanged.

## Arithmetic and operators

| operator | meaning | notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `+` `-` `*` `/` | IEEE arithmetic | result checked by the quarantine |
| `%` | floating-point remainder | `5.5 % 2` → `1.5`; checked too |
| `-x` | negation | arithmetic — checked (see below) |

### The quarantine: NaN/Inf results raise

Every arithmetic result is checked; a would-be NaN or ±Inf raises a catchable error of kind `invalid_value`:

doc.code:
1.0 / 0.0       // Error: invalid_value: float overflow or division by zero
-1.0 / 0.0      // Error: invalid_value: float overflow or division by zero
0.0 / 0.0       // Error: invalid_value: invalid float arithmetic (NaN result)
1e308 * 10.0    // Error: invalid_value: float overflow or division by zero — overflow to Inf
1.0 % 0.0       // Error: invalid_value: invalid float arithmetic (NaN result)

doc.markdown: The rule applies to sentinel *operands* too — arithmetic refuses them even though the values are storable:

doc.code:
inf = float("inf")
nan = float("nan")

inf - inf       // Error: invalid_value: invalid float arithmetic (NaN result)
inf + 1.0       // Error: invalid_value: float overflow or division by zero
nan + 1.0       // Error: invalid_value: invalid float arithmetic (NaN result)
-inf            // Error: invalid_value — unary minus is arithmetic; negate no sentinel

doc.markdown:
### Pairing with int

`float` pairs with `int` in arithmetic; the result is `float` under the same quarantine (`1 / 0.0` raises).
`float` **never pairs with `decimal` in arithmetic** — only in comparisons. Convert explicitly
(see [decimal](kavun:type/decimal)):

doc.code:
1.5 + 1       // => 2.5
1.5 + 1d      // Error: invalid_binary_operator: float + decimal — convert explicitly: 1.5.decimal() + 1d

doc.markdown:
## NaN and Inf values

The sentinels arrive from parses and hosts, never from Kavun arithmetic:

doc.code:
inf = float("inf")       // +Inf ("Infinity" and case variants parse too)
ninf = float("-inf")     // => -Inf
nan = float("nan")       // => NaN

inf.is_inf()    // => true
nan.is_nan()    // => true
(1.5).is_nan()  // => false

doc.markdown: `is_inf()` takes no sign argument — negative infinity is a composition:

doc.code:
ninf := float("-inf")
ninf.is_inf() && ninf.sign() < 0    // => true — "is it -Inf"

doc.markdown:
### Total-order comparisons

Comparison treats the whole float domain as one **total order**: NaN is the unique minimum (below even `-Inf`)
and equal only to another NaN. This keeps sorting deterministic instead of IEEE-unordered:

doc.code:
inf := float("inf")
nan := float("nan")
nan == nan                     // => true — reflexive, unlike raw IEEE
nan < float("-inf")            // => true — NaN is the unique minimum
inf > 1e308                    // => true
[2.0, nan, 1.0, inf].sort()    // => [NaN, 1.0, 2.0, +Inf]
nan == 1.0                     // => false
nan < 1                        // => false — NaN orders below numbers, not against them piecewise

doc.markdown:
### Truthiness

Truthiness is inequality with `0.0`. NaN is an error state, not a domain value — a boolean context **raises**
rather than answering:

doc.code:
(0.0).is_true()     // => false
(-0.0).is_true()    // => false
(0.5).is_true()     // => true
!!0.0               // => false
is_true(float("nan"))          // Error: invalid_value: float NaN is neither true nor false in a boolean context
float("nan").is_true()         // Error: invalid_value — the same raise: member and free spelling agree
if float("nan") {}             // Error: invalid_value — and the same raise in a condition

doc.markdown:
`float("inf").is_true()` is `true` — Inf is nonzero and has a definite answer.

## Comparisons and cross-type pairing

Cross-type `==` / `<` against `int` and `decimal` are **exact mathematical comparisons** — the float's true
stored value is compared, with no rounding of either side:

doc.code:
1 == 1.0                              // => true
0.1d == 0.1                           // => false — float 0.1 is really 0.1000000000000000055511…
0.1d < 0.1                            // => true — the decimal is below the float's true value
9007199254740993 == 9007199254740993.0   // => false — that float literal rounds to …992

doc.markdown:
`bool` / `byte` / `rune` widen to their integer value. Equality against a `string` compares the canonical text
form (`1.5 == "1.5"` → `true`, `float("nan") == "NaN"` → `true`); ordering against text raises.

## No sequence members

Scalars have no `len()`, no elements, and no `repeat`:

doc.code: (1.5).repeat(2)    // Error: invalid_method: type float has no method repeat

doc.markdown:
## Conversions

`x.T()` answers a valid `T` or raises (kind `conversion`); `x.T(default)` answers the default instead. The free
form `T(x)` is the same conversion — the default slot is the member's only; `undefined.T(d)` → `d` covers
maybe-missing data.

| target | behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `float` | identity |
| `int` | truncation toward zero for in-range values (documented resolution loss); NaN, ±Inf, and out-of-range raise-or-default |
| `decimal` | exact-enough shortest decimal (`(0.1).decimal()` → `0.1d`); NaN/±Inf raise-or-default |
| `bool` | zero test; NaN raises-or-defaults |
| `string` / `runes` | the shortest round-trip rendering (total — the default is never used) |
| `time` | unix timestamp as sec.frac — **lossy**, see [`time`](kavun:type/float/time) |

Truncation is a documented in-range resolution loss of *conversion*. **Count slots are stricter**: an argument
position that means a count, width, or edit position accepts a float only losslessly —

doc.code:
"ab".repeat(2.0)    // => "abab" — 2.0 converts losslessly
"ab".repeat(1.5)    // Error: invalid_value: (repeat) argument first must be a whole number, got 1.5

doc.markdown:
## Durations

A float builds an int **duration in nanoseconds**, rounded to the nearest one — the same members as
[int](kavun:type/int#durations): `1.5.hours()` is `5400000000000`, `0.25.seconds()` is `250000000`. NaN, ±Inf and a
result past int's range raise.

## Parsing text into float

doc.code:
float("1.5")           // => 1.5
float("inf")           // => +Inf — a parse is not arithmetic; the value is legal
float("nan")           // => NaN
float("abc")           // Error: conversion: cannot convert string to float
float("1e309")         // Error: conversion: cannot convert string to float — not representable
"abc".float(0.0)       // => 0.0 — the member's default rescues bad data
undefined.float(1.0)   // => 1.0 — the maybe-missing form
float(3)               // => 3.0

doc.markdown:
There is no `byte()` or `rune()` conversion on `float` — `int` is the sole gateway between the numeric family and
the ordinal scalars (`x.int().byte()`).

members.name: round
members.summary: Round to `n` fractional places with the rounding `mode`.

doc.markdown:
`round(n, mode)` and its fixed-mode twins `round_half_even(n)`, `round_half_up`, `round_half_down`,
`round_up`, `round_down`, `round_ceiling`, `round_floor`, plus `round_to_multiple(m, mode)` and
`round_significant(k, mode)`, are **decimal's contract**: `n` is required (negative rounds to tens,
hundreds, …), and `mode` is one of `half_even`, `half_up`, `half_down`, `up`, `down`, `ceiling`, `floor`.

A float rounds **the digits it prints** — its shortest decimal text, the one `string()` shows — not its exact
binary value. So rounding does what the reader expects from the number they see:

doc.code:
2.675.round(2, "half_up")          // => 2.68 — 2.675 is stored as 2.67499999…; it prints, and rounds, as 2.675
(0.1 + 0.2).round(1, "half_even")  // => 0.3
1234.5.round(-2, "half_up")        // => 1200.0
3.7.round_floor(0)                 // => 3.0 — floor / ceil / trunc are round_floor / round_ceiling / round_down at 0
1.234.round_to_multiple(0.05, "half_up")    // => 1.25
123456.0.round_significant(2, "half_even")  // => 120000.0
1.5.round(2, "bankers")            // Error: invalid_value: unknown rounding mode "bankers", expected one of: ceiling, …

doc.markdown:
Float rounds those digits itself, with the same seven modes as `decimal` (and, wherever `decimal` can hold the value,
exactly the same answer), so no magnitude is out of range: `1e-30.round(2, "half_up")` is `0.0`, and
`1e300.round(2, "half_up")` is `1e300` unchanged. Only a result past float's own range raises
(`1.7976931348623157e308.round(-308, "up")` would be `2e308`); NaN and ±Inf have no digits to round and raise too.

types.name: fs.file
types.summary: An open file, as `fs.open`, `fs.open_file` and `fs.create` answer it.

doc.markdown:
## Overview

`fs.file` is a handle on the world: it is owned by the [`fs`](kavun:module/fs) module, every member touches the file
system, and a refusal raises `io` naming the member (`(fs.file.read) read …: bad file descriptor`). It has no text
content, so it renders instead (`format(f)` → `<fs.file:./out.txt>`) and has no `string()`.

doc.code:
fs := import("fs")
f := fs.create("./out.txt")
f.write_string("hello")      // => 5 — the number of bytes written
f.seek(0, fs.seek_set)       // => 0
buf := bytes(b"\x00", 5)
f.read(buf)                  // => 5 — buf now holds "hello"
f.stat().size                // => 5
f.close()

doc.markdown:
## Operators

| operator | reading |
| --- | --- |
| `==` / `!=` | the same open file (identity: two opens of one path are different files) |
| `!` | a file is always truthy |
| everything else | raises |

f.close()
