members.summary: Answer the same instant viewed in UTC; see [`in_zone`](kavun:type/time/in_zone).

members.name: week_day
members.summary: Answer the day of the week, 0 (Sunday) … 6 (Saturday).

doc.code:
t := t"2026-08-29T15:04:05.123456789Z"
t.week_day()         // => 6 — Sunday is 0 … Saturday is 6

members.name: week_day_name
members.summary: Answer the English name of the day of the week.

members.name: year
members.summary: Answer the year.

members.name: year_day
members.summary: Answer the 1-based day of the year.

members.name: zone_name
members.summary: Answer the zone's abbreviation, such as `"EEST"`; see [`in_zone`](kavun:type/time/in_zone).

members.name: zone_offset
members.summary: Answer the zone's offset in seconds east of UTC; see [`in_zone`](kavun:type/time/in_zone).

types.name: undefined
types.summary: The absence of a value.

doc.markdown:
## Overview

`undefined` is what the language answers where there is nothing to answer: a missing dict key, a locator miss,
a function that returns nothing. (An **aggregation** on an empty sequence is not in that list — `[].first()`
raises, because an element can itself be `undefined` and the two cases must stay distinguishable. See
[array § Overview](kavun:type/array#overview).) It is not an error and not a zero — it is *absence*, and it
has the thinnest member surface in the language: **`format()`, `is_true()`, and the conversion members with a
mandatory default** (`undefined.int(0)` → `0` — see [Absence and defaults](kavun:type/undefined#absence-and-defaults)). Absence can
be rendered, tested, and materialized with an explicit fallback, but there is no value there to operate on —
which is why `copy` and `freeze` do not exist on it, as members or as free calls.

doc.code:
undefined.format()        // => "undefined"
undefined.is_true()       // => false
!!undefined               // => false
type_name(undefined)      // => "undefined"
is_undefined(undefined)   // => true

doc.markdown: ## Where it appears

doc.code:
d := dict({a: 1})
d["missing"]         // => undefined — a missed key
[1, 2].index(9)      // => undefined — a locator miss (never -1)

f := func() { }      // no return value
f()                  // => undefined

g := func() out { }  // a named result starts as undefined
g()                  // => undefined — until the body (or a deferred handler) assigns it

doc.markdown:
A locator miss also takes an optional trailing default that replaces the `undefined` answer:
`[1, 2].index(9, -1)` → `-1`. An aggregation on an empty sequence is not absence: it raises unless a trailing
default is given, which it then answers — `[].first(0)` → `0`.

## Operators

One rule governs everything here: `undefined` **propagates on the data plane and raises on the action plane**.
Chaining-shaped *reads* — selectors, indexing, slicing, arithmetic, concatenation, ordering — flow through and
answer `undefined`, so a chain like `a.b.c` can miss at any level and still answer one `undefined` at the end,
with no null-check flood. *Actions* — calling, membership, iteration, member calls — raise: absence performs
nothing.

On the data plane, arithmetic, concatenation, and ordering answer `undefined` rather than raising — with
equality as the one exception that answers a real `bool`:

doc.code:
undefined + 1              // => undefined
undefined + "a"            // => undefined
undefined - 1              // => undefined
undefined < 1              // => undefined — ordering has no answer against absence
undefined == undefined     // => true — the exception: equality is answerable
undefined != undefined     // => false
undefined == 0             // => false — absence equals nothing but itself
undefined && true          // => undefined
undefined || 5             // => 5 — the usual "fallback" spelling

doc.markdown: The action plane refuses instead of flowing:

Indexing and slicing both propagate (`undefined[0]` → `undefined`, `undefined[0:1]` → `undefined`) — they are
chaining-shaped reads, so a chain of lookups can miss at any level and still answer one `undefined` at the
end. And since nothing is there to mutate, `is_immutable(undefined)` answers `true`.

## Absence and defaults

`undefined` converts to nothing on its own: `int(undefined)` raises (`cannot convert undefined to int: value
is missing`). But `undefined` carries **every conversion member** — `bool`, `byte`, `rune`, `int`, `float`,
`decimal`, `time`, `date`, `string`, `runes`, `bytes`, `array`, `dict`, `record` — with a **mandatory default**, and
the member answers the default. This is the terminal step of a propagated chain — materialize the miss with a
fallback — and it replaces the test-for-undefined dance:

doc.code:
d := dict({a: 1})
d["missing"].int(0)         // => 0 — instead of: v := d["missing"]; if v == undefined { ... }
d["missing"].string("-")    // => "-"
d["a"].int(0)               // => 1 — on a present value the member is the ordinary conversion

doc.markdown:
The default is answered **as-is** — an explicit opt-out, not a type-checked replacement value
(`undefined.int("n/a")` answers `"n/a"`). *As-is* includes identity: the default is **not copied**, so a
container you pass as a default comes back as the very value you handed in, not a new one. This is the one
place a conversion member does not construct, and deliberately — the default is a value you supplied, like
the other branch of a conditional; nothing was converted, so nothing was built:

doc.code:
def := [1, 2]
got := undefined.array(def)     // got IS def — the rescue answers your value
got[0] = 9                      // def is [9, 2]
array(def)                      // ... whereas the CONVERSION always builds a new array
undefined.array(def.copy())     // say so explicitly when the default must be private

doc.markdown:
And the default is not optional here: with nothing to convert and no fallback there is nothing to answer, so
the no-default form raises:

doc.code: undefined.int()             // Error: conversion: cannot convert undefined to int: value is missing

doc.markdown:
There is no free spelling of the rescue — constructors take one value, so `int(d["missing"], 0)` raises
`wrong_num_arguments`; the default belongs to the conversion *member*.

doc.markdown:
This page is the complete, authoritative list of global built-in functions (everything callable without an
`import(...)`).

For the full list of *member* functions on each type (e.g. `[1,2,3].sort()`), see
[Detailed type documentation](kavun:doc/language#detailed-type-documentation) — this page only covers top-level
functions.

## Value constructors / conversions

`bool`, `byte`, `rune`, `int`, `float`, `decimal`, `time`, `date`, `string`, `runes`, `bytes`, `array`, `dict`,
`record`, and `range` are all callable as top-level functions named after the type. Conversion is
construction — the free form `T(x)` and the member form `x.T()` are one operation, and they share one
failure contract:

- **0 args** — the type's zero value (`int()` → `0`, `array()` → `[]`, `range()` → the empty range).
- **1 arg, already the target type** — a **new, independent value**: a constructor constructs. For the five
types with a mutable body (`array`, `dict`, `record`, `bytes`, `runes`) the result is a fresh **mutable**
**shallow** copy — exactly `x.copy_shallow()` — so `b := array(a)` never writes through to `a`, and
`bytes(b"ab")` gives a writable body built from a constant literal's content. The elements are the values
handed in, so a frozen element stays frozen; `x.copy()` is the deep spelling. `string` and the scalars are
immutable and carry no identity, so there is nothing to observe: they answer the same value.
- **1 arg, any other type** — converted. A conversion that cannot succeed **raises** a catchable error — it
never answers a silent `undefined` or a silent zero.
- **The free form calls the member.** When `x`'s type has the conversion member `x.T([default])` (a pure entry),
`T(x)` is that call, so the two spellings answer the same value or raise the same error. A type without the
member — a module-owned type as much as a builtin one — has no conversion to `T`: the free form raises. The free-only receivers are `undefined` (absence converts to
nothing), `record`, which has no members (`array(r)`, `dict(r)`, `record(r)`, and the components forms
`time(r)` / `date(r)`), and an embedder's own type, whose hooks answer when it declares no member.
- **The explicit fallback is the member form's**: `x.T(default)` answers the default instead of raising on a
failed conversion. The fallback is the *opt-out*, so it is not type-checked, and it is answered **as-is** —
a container default is **not** copied, unlike a converted value: nothing was converted, so nothing was
built. `undefined.array(def)` answers `def` itself; `array(def)` answers a new array. The free form takes
no fallback — `int("bad", 0)` raises `wrong_num_arguments`.
- **A free constructor's second argument is a construction parameter, never a default.** Only two families
take one: the sequence constructors' **count** (`T(x, n)`, below) and `time`'s / `date`'s **layout** for text
(`time("29/08/2026", "%d/%m/%Y")`). The member conversion `s.time([default])` reads the canonical grammar like
`time(s)`; the layout reading has its own member, `s.parse_time(layout[, default])` (`s.parse_date` for a
date), whose default comes after the layout; see [time.md](kavun:type/time#text-layouts).

Parsing always raises on invalid input, for every type — there is no in-band NaN-on-failed-parse:
`decimal("bad")` raises exactly like `int("bad")` does (use the member form's default when a bad parse is
expected: `"bad".decimal(0d)` → `0`).

## Building a sequence from copies: `T(x, count)`

The four sequence constructors — `array`, `string`, `bytes`, `runes` — take a second **count** argument:
`T(x, n)` builds a sequence of `n` copies of `x`, with `x` kept whole whatever its type (like `push`/`insert`,
never spreading). For the text types, whose elements are scalars, this degenerates to content repetition —
`T(x, n)` equals `T(x).repeat(n)`; for `array` it equals `[x].repeat(n)`. There is no sizing form — a single
argument is always the conversion (`array(3)` → `[3]`, `runes(10)` → `u"10"`); preallocation is the explicit
`undefined` fill:

doc.code:
array(undefined, 3)    // => [undefined, undefined, undefined] — preallocation, fill explicit
array(0, 3)            // => [0, 0, 0]
array([1, 2], 2)       // => [[1, 2], [1, 2]] — x stays whole, never spreads
bytes(b'A', 3)         // => bytes([65, 65, 65])
string("ab", 2)        // => "abab"
runes("ab", 2)         // => u"abab"
array(3)               // => [3] — arity 1 is the conversion, never a size
runes(10)              // => u"10"
array([1, 2])          // => [1, 2] — passthrough
array(range(1, 4))     // => [1, 2, 3] — conversion

doc.markdown:
The count must be a lossless whole number (`2.0` is fine, `1.5` raises) and non-negative (a negative count
raises a recoverable `invalid_value` error); a count of `0` answers the empty sequence.

## `dict`/`record` are outliers

`dict()` and `record()` — mirror images, converting in opposite directions — follow the shared convention above
(the zero value, a same-type copy, a raise on any other type) and add two shapes of their own: the `_view`
constructors, which share storage instead of copying, and the entries form, which builds from an array of
`[key, value]` pairs:

- `dict()` / `record()` — empty dict / record.
- `dict(d)` / `record(r)` where the argument is already the target type — a new, independent shallow copy, as
every constructor answers.
- `dict(r)` where `r` is a `record`, and `record(d)` where `d` is a `dict` — converted to an independent
**shallow** copy: a fresh top-level container, but nested values are not recursively cloned (same convention
every other type's own `.record()`/`.dict()` conversion already follows). Mutating the result's own keys never
affects the source's keys, or vice versa; mutating a *nested* container reachable from both still affects both
(shallow, not deep). Result is always mutable, regardless of the source's mutability — same convention as
`copy()`.
- `dict_view(r)` / `record_view(d)` are the explicit `_view` twins: share the source's underlying storage
directly instead of copying — both the top-level key set and nested values are the *same* backing map, so
mutating either side through either wrapper is visible through both. Result's mutability is inherited from
the source's (shares its immutability, not always-mutable like the copying form). Maximum performance when
you've confirmed nothing else needs to observe the source independently.
- `dict(entries)` / `record(entries)` where `entries` is an array — the ENTRIES reading: each element must be
exactly a 2-element array `[key, value]` (`dict([["a", 1]])` → `dict({"a": 1})`); keys go through their
string conversion, later entries overwrite earlier ones. The same reading powers `arr.dict()` and
`d.array()` (which answers key-sorted entries), so the two directions round-trip up to ordering.
- `dict(x)` / `record(x)` for any other type — **raises a runtime error**, like every failed conversion.

The same member-call spellings exist on the relevant receiver: `dict_val.record()` / `dict_val.record_view()`.
`record` has no member functions at all (a dot on a record is field access — see `docs/reference/types/record.md`),
so `record_val.dict()` doesn't exist; `dict(record_val)`/`dict_view(record_val)` are its only spellings for that
direction.

doc.code:
dict()                 // => dict({})
dict({a: 1})            // => dict({"a": 1}) — from record, independent shallow copy
record(dict({a: 1}))    // => {"a": 1} — from dict, independent shallow copy
dict_view({a: 1})       // => dict({"a": 1}) — shares storage with the record literal
dict(42)                // Error: conversion: cannot convert int to dict

doc.markdown:
## Collections and helpers

A free function exists exactly where a member cannot do the job: nullary construction (`int()`), a multi-input
subject (`min(a, b, c)` selects among its ARGUMENTS; `arr.min()` aggregates over elements — one meaning, two
delivery mechanisms), or a receiver that cannot have members — `record` has no member surface at all, which is
why `len`, the copy/freeze family, `remove`/`remove_in_place`, `format`, `is_true` and `is_view` all keep free
spellings. A free form that would merely duplicate a member does not exist (there is no free `append`).

## Type predicates

Each `is_T` predicate (except `is_callable`/`is_iterable`/`is_immutable`) checks the value's *exact*
runtime type — no coercion, and no "is-a" relationship between related types (e.g. `is_int(byte(1))` is `false`).

functions.name: array
functions.summary: Convert `x` to an `array`, or build `count` copies of it as elements; with no argument, `[]`.

doc.code: array([1, 2])         // => [1, 2] — a NEW array: writing into it never touches the argument

functions.name: bool
functions.summary: Convert `x` to a `bool` — exactly `x.bool()`; with no argument, `false`.

doc.code:
bool(0.0)             // => false — bool(x) is a numeric zero test / text parse
bool("false")         // => false — parses; distinct from is_true("false"), which is true (non-empty)

functions.name: byte
functions.summary: Convert `x` to a `byte` — exactly `x.byte()`; with no argument, `byte(0)`.

doc.code: byte(999)             // Error: conversion — out of the octet range

functions.name: bytes
functions.summary: Convert `x` to `bytes`, or build `count` copies of it; with no argument, empty `bytes`.

doc.code: bytes(b"ab")          // => bytes([97, 98]) — mutable; the literal itself stays an immutable constant

functions.name: copy
functions.summary: Answer a deep, mutable copy of `x`.

doc.code: copy(x)                                      // deep mutable copy

doc.markdown: `copy`/`freeze` work on every type except `undefined` (absence has no identity to copy).

functions.name: copy_shallow
functions.summary: Answer a shallow, mutable copy of an `array`, `dict` or `record`.

doc.code: copy_shallow(x)                              // shallow mutable copy (array/dict/record only — elsewhere unobservable)

functions.name: date
functions.summary: Convert `x` to a `date`, or read `text` under a `layout`; with no argument, `1970-01-01`.

functions.name: decimal
functions.summary: Convert `x` to a `decimal`; with no argument, `0d`.

doc.code: decimal("bad")        // Error: conversion — parse always raises on invalid input

functions.name: dict
functions.summary: Convert `x` to a `dict`; with no argument, the empty dict; see [the outliers](kavun:builtins#dictrecord-are-outliers).

functions.name: dict_view
functions.summary: Answer a `dict` sharing a record's storage; see [the outliers](kavun:builtins#dictrecord-are-outliers).

functions.name: error
functions.summary: Wrap `payload` as an error value; with `fatal` true, raising it bypasses every `recover()`.

doc.code:
error("msg")                                 // error value with a string payload
error({code: 42})                            // error value with a structured payload

doc.markdown:
`error(...)` requires at least one argument (an error without a payload carries no information — and note every
error value is truthy).

functions.name: float
functions.summary: Convert `x` to a `float`; with no argument, `0.0`.

functions.name: format
functions.summary: Render one value, or fill a template's placeholders from `args`.

doc.code: format(x); format(template, args)            // render one value / runtime template formatting (see below)

format("hello {x} from {y}!", {x: "Kavun", y: "Kherson"})  // => "hello Kavun from Kherson!"
format("hello {0} from {1}!", ["Kavun", "Kherson"])        // => "hello Kavun from Kherson!"
format("pi = {x:.3f}", {x: 3.14159})                       // => "pi = 3.142"
format("n = {x:{fmt}}", {x: 42, fmt: "05d"})               // => "n = 00042"

doc.markdown:
`format(template, args)` is the runtime counterpart to f-strings. The template uses the same `{name}` / `{0}`
placeholder syntax and the same [Format Mini-Language](kavun:doc/format_mini_language) for `:fspec`. `args` must be an
`array` (for indexed placeholders) or a `dict` / `record` (for named placeholders); the two modes cannot be mixed
in one template, and expressions are not allowed inside `{...}`. See [`format`](kavun:doc/format_function) for the full
reference.

functions.name: freeze
functions.summary: Answer a deep-immutable copy of `x`, leaving the source untouched.

doc.code: freeze(x)                                    // deep copy, then deep-immutable; source untouched

doc.markdown:
`freeze`/`freeze_shallow` differ in shape because immutability lives on the value header, not the shared body:
`freeze(x)` detaches first (a deep copy) and marks the clone immutable, never affecting other bindings;
`freeze_shallow(x)` returns `x` with its own header flagged — the caller must reassign
(`x = freeze_shallow(x)`), and a sibling binding that still points at the same body stays mutable.

functions.name: freeze_shallow
functions.summary: Answer `x` with its own header marked immutable; see [`freeze`](kavun:builtin/freeze).

doc.code: freeze_shallow(x)                            // x, header marked immutable; needs `x = freeze_shallow(x)` to stick

functions.name: int
functions.summary: Convert `x` to an `int`; with no argument, `0`.

doc.code:
int("42")             // => 42
int("bad")            // Error: conversion: cannot convert string to int
"bad".int(0)          // => 0 — explicit fallback: the member form's trailing default

functions.name: is_array
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly an `array`, with no coercion.

doc.code: is_array([1, 2])   // => true

functions.name: is_bool
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly a `bool`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_byte
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly a `byte`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_bytes
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly a `bytes`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_callable
functions.summary: Report whether `x` can be called, host-defined callable types included; see [`is_function`](kavun:builtin/is_function).

doc.code: is_callable(len)   // => true

functions.name: is_date
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly a `date`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_decimal
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly a `decimal`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_dict
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly a `dict`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_error
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly an `error`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_float
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly a `float`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_function
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is a function: `type_name(x) == "function"`.

doc.markdown:
`is_function(x)` is the type predicate (`type_name(x) == "function"`, true for functions, closures and builtin
functions alike); `is_callable(x)` is the capability predicate — it additionally covers host-defined callable
types, which keep their own `type_name`.

functions.name: is_immutable
functions.summary: Report whether `x` cannot be mutated through this reference.

doc.markdown:
`is_immutable(x)` answers true unless the value can be mutated **through that reference** — it reads
the header, exceptionlessly, so `is_immutable(undefined)` is `true`. It is not a promise that the content
cannot change: a frozen header over a body something else still owns (a frozen view, or any
`freeze_shallow`ed sibling) refuses *your* writes while the other holder's writes remain visible through it —
see [container semantics: views](kavun:doc/container_semantics#views).

functions.name: is_int
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly an `int`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_iterable
functions.summary: Report whether `x` can be iterated with `for … in`.

functions.name: is_range
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly a `range`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_record
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly a `record`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_rune
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly a `rune`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_runes
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly a `runes`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_string
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly a `string`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_time
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is exactly a `time`, with no coercion.

functions.name: is_true
functions.summary: Report the truthiness of `x`, the free spelling of `x.is_true()`.

doc.code: is_true(x)                                   // truthiness (the free spelling of x.is_true())

functions.name: is_undefined
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is `undefined`.

functions.name: is_view
functions.summary: Report whether `x` is a borrowing header — a `_view` result.

doc.code: is_view(x)                                   // is x a borrowing header — a `_view` result?

doc.markdown:
`is_view(x)` reports whether `x` is a **borrowing header** — a value produced by
`slice_view`/`chunk_view`/`dict_view`/`record_view`, which reads and writes another value's body instead of
owning one. It is a property of `x` alone: it does not say whether anything is viewing `x` (after
`r = d.record_view()`, `is_view(r)` is `true` and `is_view(d)` is `false`), and it is not a general "is this
body shared" test — plain assignment (`e := d`) and `freeze_shallow` also share a body without producing a
view.

functions.name: len
functions.summary: Answer the length of a collection, text or range.

doc.code: len(x)                                       // length of a collection/text/range; raises on types with no length

doc.markdown: `len(x)` raises on a type with no length — it never answers a made-up number.

functions.name: max
functions.summary: Answer the largest argument; see [`min`](kavun:builtin/min).

functions.name: min
functions.summary: Answer the smallest argument.

doc.code: min(a, b, ...); max(a, b, ...)               // smallest/largest ARGUMENT (see below)

doc.markdown: `min`/`max` are variadic selection over their **arguments** — deliberately never looking inside one:

doc.code:
min(3, 1, 2)           // => 1
min("banana", "apple") // => "apple"
min([3, 1, 2])         // => [3, 1, 2] — ONE argument, returned unchanged; not a lookup inside it
min([3, 1, 2]...)      // => 1 — spread it, which always agrees with [3, 1, 2].min()
min()                  // Error: wrong_num_arguments — there is nothing to select

functions.name: raise
functions.summary: Raise `err` — wrapped as an error first if it is not one — so a deferred `recover()` can catch it.

doc.code: raise(err)                                   // raise an error so a deferred recover() can catch it

functions.name: range
functions.summary: Build a `range`: empty with no argument, from a components record, or from `start`, `stop` and an optional `step`.

doc.code: range({start: 1, stop: 4})  // => range(1, 4) — rebuilds from a components record
range(0, 10)                                 // range(start, stop[, step]) — sugar: 0..10, 0..10:step

functions.name: record
functions.summary: Convert `x` to a `record`; with no argument, the empty record; see [the outliers](kavun:builtins#dictrecord-are-outliers).

functions.name: record_view
functions.summary: Answer a `record` sharing a dict's storage; see [the outliers](kavun:builtins#dictrecord-are-outliers).

functions.name: recover
functions.summary: Inside a deferred function, answer the in-flight error and stop the unwinding; otherwise `undefined`.

doc.code: recover()                                    // inside a deferred function, return & clear the in-flight error

doc.markdown: It must be called directly inside the deferred function — any indirection answers `undefined`.

functions.name: remove
functions.summary: Answer a `dict` or `record` without `key`, leaving `obj` untouched.

doc.code: remove(obj, "key")                           // returns obj without "key"; does not mutate obj

functions.name: remove_in_place
functions.summary: Remove `key` from a `dict` or `record` in place; see [`remove`](kavun:builtin/remove).

doc.code: remove_in_place(obj, "key")                  // mutates a record/dict in place

functions.name: require
functions.summary: Answer `undefined` when `cond` is true; otherwise raise a recoverable error of kind `requirement` carrying `payload` untouched.

doc.code: require(cond, payload)                       // input check: undefined if cond is true, else raise kind "requirement"

functions.name: rune
functions.summary: Convert `x` to a `rune`; with no argument, NUL.

doc.markdown:
An `int` converts iff it is in the rune domain. A `byte` always converts, read as text: an ASCII octet is that
symbol, a higher one its octet escape — the inverse of `rune.byte()`.

doc.code:
rune(65)             // => 'A'
rune(b'A')           // => 'A'
rune(b'\xe9')        // => '\udce9' — the octet's escape, never U+00E9
rune(b'\xe9').byte() // => byte(233)
rune(55296)          // Error: conversion

functions.name: runes
functions.summary: Convert `x` to `runes`, or build `count` copies of it; with no argument, empty `runes`.

doc.code: runes("abc")          // => u"abc"

functions.name: string
functions.summary: Convert `x` to a `string`, or build `count` copies of it; with no argument, `""`.

doc.code:
string(99)            // => "99"
string(bytes([0x61, 0x80])) // => "a\x80" — total: the octets as they are, exactly .string()
string(undefined)     // Error: conversion — absence has no textual form

functions.name: time
functions.summary: Convert `x` to a `time`, or read `text` under a `layout`; with no argument, the zero time (unix 0, UTC).

doc.code:
time("2024-01-01")    // time value (the canonical grammar; anything else names its layout)
time("01/02/2024", "%d/%m/%Y")  // time value -- the second argument is the layout

functions.name: type_name
functions.summary: Answer the runtime type name of `x` (`"function"` for every callable).

doc.code: type_name({})      // => "record"

modules.name: base64
modules.summary: Base64 encoding and decoding: the standard and URL-safe alphabets, with or without padding.

doc.markdown: Example:

doc.code:
base64 = import("base64")
base64.encode(bytes("hello"))

doc.markdown:
**Failures.** A malformed input raises kind `conversion`, with the function name in the message: `(base64.decode)
illegal base64 data at input byte 0`.

functions.name: decode
functions.summary: Decode standard Base64 text.

doc.markdown: `s` is a `string`.

functions.name: encode
functions.summary: Encode `data` as standard Base64.

doc.markdown: `data` is `bytes`.

functions.name: raw_decode
functions.summary: Decode standard Base64 text written without padding.

doc.markdown: `s` is a `string`.

functions.name: raw_encode
functions.summary: Encode `data` as standard Base64 without padding.

doc.markdown: `data` is `bytes`.

functions.name: raw_url_decode
functions.summary: Decode URL-safe Base64 text written without padding.

doc.markdown: `s` is a `string`.

functions.name: raw_url_encode
functions.summary: Encode `data` as URL-safe Base64 without padding.

doc.markdown: `data` is `bytes`.

functions.name: url_decode
functions.summary: Decode URL-safe Base64 text.

doc.markdown: `s` is a `string`.

functions.name: url_encode
functions.summary: Encode `data` as URL-safe Base64.

doc.markdown: `data` is `bytes`.

modules.name: clock
modules.summary: The world's time: the current instant, the distance to one, and waiting.

doc.markdown: It is the only place a script reads the wall clock, so it needs a grant.

doc.code:
clock := import("clock")
clock.now().in_zone("Europe/Kyiv").format("#datetime")
start := clock.now()
clock.sleep(10.milliseconds())
clock.since(start).in_seconds()     // ≈ 0.01

doc.markdown:
Durations are **int members**, not module functions: `30.seconds()`, `1.5.hours()`, `d.in_minutes()`,
`d.duration_string()`, `"1h30m".nanoseconds()` (see [reference/types/int.md § Durations](kavun:type/int#durations)).
Construction, parsing, zones, calendar arithmetic and calendar facts are on the `time` and `date` types —
`time(…)`, `t.in_zone(z)`, `t.add_months(n, rule)`, `t.is_leap_year()`.

**Failures.** An argument that does not convert to `time` (`since`, `until`) or to an `int` duration (`sleep`)
raises kind `invalid_argument_type`; a wrong count, `wrong_num_arguments`.

functions.name: now
functions.summary: Answer the current instant, in UTC.

functions.name: since
functions.summary: Answer the duration from `t` to now, in nanoseconds.

functions.name: sleep
functions.summary: Wait `d` nanoseconds (`clock.sleep(2.seconds())`).

functions.name: until
functions.summary: Answer the duration from now to `t`, in nanoseconds.

doc.code:
exec := import("exec")
string(exec.exec("echo", "hi").output())   // => "hi\n" — output() answers bytes
p := exec.start_process("/bin/sleep", ["sleep", "0"], "", [])
p.wait().success                        // => true

doc.markdown:
The two types are documented on their own pages: [`exec.command`](kavun:type/exec.command) (`run`, `start`, `wait`,
`output`, `combined_output`, `set_path`, `set_dir`, `set_env`, `process`) and
[`exec.process`](kavun:type/exec.process) (`pid`, `kill`, `signal`, `wait`, `release`). `process.wait()` answers a
frozen record of facts: `{pid, exited, success, status}`.

**Failures.** A program that cannot be found or run, or ends badly for `run`/`output`, raises `io` naming the call
(`(exec.command.run) exit status 1`).

functions.name: exec
functions.summary: Prepare a command; configure it, then run it once.

doc.markdown: `name` is a `string`.

functions.name: exec_look_path
functions.summary: Search `PATH` for an executable named `file`.

doc.markdown: `file` is a `string`.

functions.name: find_process
functions.summary: Answer the process with that pid.

doc.markdown: `pid` is an `int`.

functions.name: start_process
functions.summary: Start a process.

doc.markdown: `name` is a `string`, `argv` is an array of strings, `dir` is a `string` and `env` is an array of strings.

modules.name: fin
modules.summary: Deterministic financial arithmetic — time value of money, cashflows, depreciation, rate conversion — backed by [fin128](https://github.com/jokruger/fin128) over the same dec128 library `decimal` uses.

doc.markdown:
Every function either answers an exact `decimal` at the rounding you stated or raises; nothing is approximated,
nothing defaults.

doc.code:
fin := import("fin")
fin.payment(0.005d, 60, 25000, 0, "arrears", 2, "half_even")   // => -483.32d — a 60-month loan at 0.5% a month

doc.markdown:
**The argument contract**, shared by every function:

- Money, rates and factors are `decimal` or `int`. A `float` **raises** (`argument rate expects type decimal or
int, got float`) — binary floating point cannot spell most decimal rates, and an approximate rate is a wrong
posting. Counts (`n`, `period`, `life`, `m`, `num`, `den`) are `int`.
- Every quantizing function **ends with `(scale, mode)`**, read exactly as `decimal`'s `*_round` members read
them: scale 0…19, mode one of `ceiling`, `floor`, `down`, `up`, `half_down`, `half_up`, `half_even`. There is no
default scale or mode.
- Enum arguments are **exact canonical names** (case-sensitive): `timing` is `"arrears"` (payments at period end)
or `"advance"` (at period start); `frequency` is `"annual"`, `"semiannual"`, `"quarterly"`, `"monthly"`,
`"weekly"` or `"daily"`. An unknown name raises and lists the accepted ones.
- Sign convention: money flowing **in** is positive, **out** negative — a positive `pv` (the amount borrowed)
gives a negative `payment` (the amount paid back).
- The solver-driven functions (`rate`, `irr`) take an optional **solver spec** just before `(scale, mode)`: a
record or dict with any of `lo`, `hi` (the search bracket), `tolerance` (in ulps at the output scale) and
`max_iter`, laid over the frozen defaults `fin.default_solver()` answers (`{lo: -0.9999d, hi: 9, tolerance: 1,
max_iter: 100}`). An unknown key raises. The solver is bisection, so its answer depends only on the bracket and
the tolerance.

**Failures.** Data the formula cannot use raises `invalid_value` with fin128's reason —
`(fin.payment) the number of periods must be positive`, `(fin.irr) the bracket does not contain a root`,
`(fin.straight_line) the salvage value is above the cost`. A wrong argument type raises `invalid_argument_type`,
a wrong count `wrong_num_arguments`, a division by zero `division_by_zero`.

## Function groups

Each group's functions, linked to their entries:

| group | functions |
| --- | --- |
| time value of money | [`payment`](kavun:module/fin/payment), [`present_value`](kavun:module/fin/present_value), [`future_value`](kavun:module/fin/future_value), [`periods`](kavun:module/fin/periods) → `[whole, remainder]`, [`rate`](kavun:module/fin/rate), [`annuity_factor_pv`](kavun:module/fin/annuity_factor_pv), [`annuity_factor_fv`](kavun:module/fin/annuity_factor_fv) |
| schedule (period `1…n`) | [`balance`](kavun:module/fin/balance) — the balance after the period; [`charge_part`](kavun:module/fin/charge_part) / [`principal_part`](kavun:module/fin/principal_part) — the period payment's interest and principal parts |
| cashflows | [`npv`](kavun:module/fin/npv), [`irr`](kavun:module/fin/irr), [`mirr`](kavun:module/fin/mirr) — `cf` is an array of `decimal\|int`, one per period |
| depreciation | [`straight_line`](kavun:module/fin/straight_line), [`sum_of_digits`](kavun:module/fin/sum_of_digits), [`declining_balance`](kavun:module/fin/declining_balance), [`declining_rate_from_factor`](kavun:module/fin/declining_rate_from_factor), [`declining_rate_from_salvage`](kavun:module/fin/declining_rate_from_salvage) |
| rates and factors | [`nominal_to_effective`](kavun:module/fin/nominal_to_effective), [`effective_to_nominal`](kavun:module/fin/effective_to_nominal) (`m` compounding periods a year), [`compound_factor`](kavun:module/fin/compound_factor), [`discount_factor`](kavun:module/fin/discount_factor), [`per_year`](kavun:module/fin/per_year) → `int` |
| day count | [`year_fraction`](kavun:module/fin/year_fraction) (the constructor), [`year_fraction_between`](kavun:module/fin/year_fraction_between), [`year_fraction_between_final`](kavun:module/fin/year_fraction_between_final), [`days_between`](kavun:module/fin/days_between), [`days_between_final`](kavun:module/fin/days_between_final), [`days_in_year`](kavun:module/fin/days_in_year), [`conventions`](kavun:module/fin/conventions), [`is_year_fraction`](kavun:module/fin/is_year_fraction) — see [fin.year_fraction](kavun:type/fin.year_fraction) |
| interest over a fraction | [`accrue_simple`](kavun:module/fin/accrue_simple), [`accrue_compound`](kavun:module/fin/accrue_compound), [`compound_factor_for`](kavun:module/fin/compound_factor_for), [`discount_factor_for`](kavun:module/fin/discount_factor_for) |
| discount instruments | [`discount_price`](kavun:module/fin/discount_price), [`discount_rate`](kavun:module/fin/discount_rate), [`discount_yield`](kavun:module/fin/discount_yield) |
| dated cashflows | [`xnpv`](kavun:module/fin/xnpv), [`xirr`](kavun:module/fin/xirr) — `flows` is an array of `{date, amount}`, ascending by date |
| rate and charge tables | [`tiered_rates`](kavun:module/fin/tiered_rates), [`tiered_charges`](kavun:module/fin/tiered_charges), [`dated_rates`](kavun:module/fin/dated_rates), [`dated_charges`](kavun:module/fin/dated_charges), and [`is_tiered_rates`](kavun:module/fin/is_tiered_rates) … — see [Rate and charge tables](kavun:module/fin#rate-and-charge-tables) |
| exact helpers | [`apply_rate`](kavun:module/fin/apply_rate) (amount × rate, rounded once), [`exact_product`](kavun:module/fin/exact_product) (exact, or raises), [`mul_div_round`](kavun:module/fin/mul_div_round) (a × b × num / den, rounded once) |
| units (exact) | [`to_percent`](kavun:module/fin/to_percent), [`from_percent`](kavun:module/fin/from_percent), [`to_basis_points`](kavun:module/fin/to_basis_points), [`from_basis_points`](kavun:module/fin/from_basis_points) |
| solver | [`root`](kavun:module/fin/root) — x where `f(x) = 0`; [`brackets`](kavun:module/fin/brackets) → `bool`; [`default_solver`](kavun:module/fin/default_solver) → record |

Spreadsheet equivalents, for migrations: `payment` ≈ `PMT`, `present_value` ≈ `PV`, `future_value` ≈ `FV`,
`periods` ≈ `NPER` (split into whole periods and a remainder), `rate` ≈ `RATE`, `charge_part` ≈ `IPMT`,
`principal_part` ≈ `PPMT`, `straight_line` ≈ `SLN`, `sum_of_digits` ≈ `SYD`. **`npv` is not the spreadsheet's
`NPV`**: here `cf[0]` sits at t = 0 and is not discounted (the definition, as numpy-financial has it); a
spreadsheet discounts its first value by one period. Pass the initial outlay as `cf[0]`, or shift the array.

Quantize then recompute: a function's result is already rounded to the scale you asked for, and each function
rounds its own result once. So two results rounded independently — `balance` and `principal_part` of the same
period — can disagree by a cent with their difference. Build a schedule from **one** rounded series and derive the
rest from it (see [the loan example](kavun:doc/examples#a-loan-schedule-with-fin)).

## Day count

**Conventions** are named by their market spelling and read through fin128's alias table, so `"ACT/365F"`,
`"30/360 US"` or `"Actual/360"` work as products store them; `fin.conventions()` lists the canonical names
(`30B/360`, `30E-ISDA/360`, `30E/360`, `30E3/360`, `30U/360`, `ACT/360`, `ACT/365`, `ACT/366`, `ACT/ACT`,
`NL/365`). An unknown name raises and lists them. The `_final` variants take `end` as the contract's termination
date — only `30E-ISDA/360` distinguishes it, when the termination falls at the end of February.

`days_between` and `days_in_year` answer the **convention's** count, not the calendar's:
`fin.days_between(d"2026-02-01", d"2026-03-01", "30E/360")` is `30` (the calendar's `d2 - d1` is `28`), and
`fin.days_in_year(d"2028-03-01", "ACT/360")` is `360` (the calendar's `d"2028-03-01".days_in_year()` is `366`).

**Dated cashflows** discount each flow by the year fraction from the **first** flow's date, so the flows must be in
ascending date order — an unsorted array raises rather than being sorted for you:

Each flow is a record or dict with exactly `date` (a `date`) and `amount` (`decimal|int`).

Not yet available: conventions outside the named set (a custom year length, a host-defined name table, a
script-defined convention) — a stated fraction, `fin.year_fraction(n, d)`, covers the functions that take `f`.

## The solver: `root` and `brackets`

`fin.root(f, [solver,] scale, mode)` finds the `x` where a function crosses zero, by bisection over the
solver bracket — the same solver `rate`, `irr` and `xirr` use, so its answer depends only on the bracket and the
tolerance. `fin.brackets(f[, solver])` answers whether `f` changes sign across the bracket at all: it tells a
bracket that merely missed (widen `hi`) from a function with no root.

doc.code:
fin := import("fin")
flows := [{date: d"2026-01-01", amount: -10000}, {date: d"2026-06-30", amount: 2750},
          {date: d"2027-01-01", amount: 4250}, {date: d"2027-06-30", amount: 3250},
          {date: d"2028-01-01", amount: 2750}]
fin.root(x => x * x - 2, 10, "half_even")                     // => 1.4142135624d
fin.root(r => fin.xnpv(r, flows, "ACT/365F", 12, "half_even"), 10, "half_even")   // xirr, spelled out
fin.brackets(x => x - 20)                                     // => false — the default bracket stops at 9
fin.root(x => x - 20, {hi: 50}, 10, "half_even")              // => 20.0000000000d

doc.markdown:
The callback contract:

- `f` is any callable that **accepts one argument** — `func(x)`, `func(x, ...rest)`, `func(...args)`, a builtin or
a bound member that does (`decimal`, `1d.copy_sign`); one that does not raises `invalid_argument_type`, and a
lambda adapts it (`x => g(x, 2)`). It is called with a `decimal` and returns a `decimal` or `int` — anything else
raises `invalid_argument_type`.
- A raise inside `f` stops the search and surfaces **as itself** — the script sees its own error, never "the bracket
does not contain a root". After the first raise `f` is not called again. A fatal error (`stack_overflow`) stays
fatal.
- `f` is called at most `max_iter + 2` times (102 with the defaults).
- `f` may itself call `fin.root`. The result is deterministic only if `f` is: a callback that reads the clock or
other host state makes the answer depend on it. Calls that run a callback are never folded at compile time.

## Rate and charge tables

Four immutable, validated table types for product parameters — a savings ladder, a fee schedule, a teaser rate
that reverts, a standing charge that changes on a date. Each is built once, from a one-line **text form** (what a
product configuration stores) or from **band records** (when a script computes the table), and then asked
questions. Like `fin.year_fraction`, each type is named after its constructor.

| type | text form | band record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fin.tiered_rates` | `"0:0.005, 1000:0.007, 10000:0.009"` — from 0, open at the top | `{from, rate}` |
| `fin.tiered_charges` | `"0:0.015+2.00, 1000:0.01; min=25, max=500"` — a rate plus a fixed amount per band, the charge clamped | `{from, rate, fixed}`, with `(bands, min, max)`; `max` 0 = no cap |
| `fin.dated_rates` | `"2026-01-01:0.04, 2026-07-01:0.02"` — each band from a date to the next | `{from: date, rate}` |
| `fin.dated_charges` | `"2024-01-01:25.00, 2025-01-01:30.00"` | `{from: date, amount}` |

A rate is written as a rate, never a percent (`0.007` is 0.7%), and the digits are kept as written (`"0:0.50"`
stays `"0:0.50"`). Values are `decimal|int` — a `float` raises. Every ordering and anchoring rule (ascending
bands, the first tiered band at 0, `max` not below `min`) is fin128's, and raises the same way from text or
records. The empty text raises: a table always has a band.

`rule` is `"whole"` (the band the amount lands in applies to all of it) or `"marginal"` (each slice at its own
band's rate). A member a table does not have does not exist: `tc.rate(…)` is `invalid_method` (a fixed charge is
money, not a rate), as is `dc.apply(…)`.

**Values, not containers.** A table has no `len()`, iteration, indexing or `in`; `for b in t.bands()` reads it.
`bands()` answers the records in constructor shape, so `fin.tiered_rates(t.bands()) == t`. Two tables are equal
when they have the same bands, compared numerically (`"0:0.50"` equals `"0:0.5"`; for `tiered_charges` the bounds
too) — but `"0:0, 1000:0"` is **not** `"0:0"`: under `"marginal"` an extra band changes the parts. There is no
ordering. Each type's default (`fin.tiered_rates()` …) is the zero-rate table (`"0:0"`, or `"0001-01-01:0"` for the
dated ones), the one falsy table.

**In configuration**, store the text form: `json.encode` writes a table as its text, and `json.decode` gives the
string back for `fin.tiered_rates(cfg.rates)`. (JSON numbers decode as `float`, which the record form refuses.)

modules.name: fs
modules.summary: The file system: files, directories, links, permissions.

doc.code:
fs := import("fs")
f := fs.create("./out.txt")
f.write_string("hello")
f.close()
string(fs.read_file("./out.txt"))   // => "hello" — read_file answers bytes
fs.stat("./out.txt").size           // => 5

doc.markdown:
The constants are the flags of [`open_file`](kavun:module/fs/open_file), combined with `|`; the whence of
[`fs.file.seek`](kavun:type/fs.file/seek); and the bits of a file mode, the `mode` of [`stat`](kavun:module/fs/stat).

An open file is an [`fs.file`](kavun:type/fs.file): `name`, `read(buffer)`, `write(bytes)`, `write_string(s)`,
`seek(offset, whence)`, `stat`, `sync`, `chmod`, `chown`, `chdir`, `read_dir_names(n)`, `close`.

**Failures.** Everything the world can refuse raises kind `io`, with the operation named in the message:
`(fs.remove) remove /nope: no such file or directory`. A function whose success has no result answers `undefined`.

modules.name: io
modules.summary: The script's console: print, write and read on the VM's standard streams.

doc.markdown:
It writes to the VM's stdout and reads from its stdin — the process streams unless the host redirects them
(`VM.SetStdout`, `VM.SetStdin`, see [embedding.md § Standard streams](kavun:doc/embedding#standard-streams)).

| | line-oriented | raw stream |
| --- | --- | --- |
| output | `print(...values)` | `write(...values)` |
| input | `read_line([default])` | `read([n])` |

Example:

doc.code:
io := import("io")
io.print("sum:", 20 + 22)            // sum: 42
io.write("a", "b"); io.write("c\n")  // abc
name := io.read_line("anonymous")    // one line of input, or "anonymous" at end of input
head := io.read(4)                   // the next 4 symbols ("" at end of input)
rest := io.read()                    // everything after them ("" when nothing is left)

doc.markdown:
Both readers share one input buffer, so `read_line` followed by `read` loses nothing. Octets that are not valid
UTF-8 come through unchanged; each counts as one symbol, as in every text conversion.

Failures: `io` (an output or input stream the world refused, or end of input for `read_line` without a default);
`invalid_value` (a negative count); `invalid_argument_type`; `wrong_num_arguments`.

functions.name: print
functions.summary: Print the values separated by spaces, then a newline.

doc.markdown: Text prints as its content, everything else as its render.

functions.name: read
functions.summary: Read the rest of the input, or with `n`, the next `n` symbols.

doc.markdown:
Without `n`, the rest of the input. With `n`, the next `n` symbols — the unit of a string's `len()` and indexing —
waiting for them unless the input ends first, so it answers fewer only at end of input. `""` only at end of input
(and for `n == 0`), so a loop `for s := io.read(64); s != ""; s = io.read(64)` ends cleanly. A negative `n` raises
`invalid_value`; `n` bounds the read, it is not an allocation.

functions.name: read_line
functions.summary: Read one line of input without its terminator (`\n` or `\r\n`).

doc.markdown:
A last line with no terminator is still a line. At end of input it raises `io` (`(io.read_line) end of input`),
unless a default is given — then the default is answered as-is. (`""` is a valid line, so end of input cannot answer
it.)

functions.name: write
functions.summary: Write the values concatenated — no separator, no newline.

doc.markdown: The building block for output assembled piece by piece.

modules.name: json
modules.summary: JSON encoding and decoding of Kavun values.

doc.markdown: Example:

doc.code:
json = import("json")
json.encode({"a": 1, "b": true})

doc.markdown:
**Failures.** `decode` and `indent` raise kind `json_decoding` on malformed input. `decode` reads a number without a
fraction or exponent as `int` and any other as `float`, and raises `json_decoding` when it does not fit — an integer
outside int64 (`(json.decode) number 9223372036854775808 is out of int range`) or a float that would be ±Inf
(`1e999`); it never wraps or clamps. A host passing JSON it decoded itself (`json.Number` through `kavun.ValueOf`)
gets the same rule — [embedding.md § Converting Go values](kavun:doc/embedding#converting-go-values). `encode` raises
kind `json_encoding` on a value with no JSON representation, naming the path to it once — `.items[0].price: value
type <compiled-function/0> does not support JSON encoding` — and on text holding octets that are not symbols (JSON is
UTF-8 by definition; encode such text as `bytes`, which goes as base64).

functions.summary: Decode JSON text (`bytes` or `string`) into a Kavun value.

doc.markdown: `data` is `bytes` or a `string`.

functions.summary: Encode a Kavun value as JSON bytes.

modules.name: math
modules.summary: Constants, trigonometry and the special functions.

doc.markdown:
A numeric operation that `decimal` has is a **float member** instead — `x.sqrt()`, `x.pow(y)`, `x.exp()`, `x.ln()`,
`x.log2()`, `x.log10()`, `x.round(n, mode)` and its twins, `x.copy_sign(y)`, `x.quo_rem(y)`, … (see
[reference/types/float.md § Overview](kavun:type/float#overview)) — so no function exists both ways. `min`/`max` are
not module functions either: selection over arguments is the free variadic `min(a, b, ...)` / `max(a, b, ...)`, and
aggregation over elements is the member (`arr.min()`).

Example:

doc.code:
math = import("math")
math.hypot(3, 4)       // => 5.0
math.cbrt(27)          // => 3.0
math.pi                // => 3.141592653589793

doc.markdown:
The constants are the numeric constants [`pi`](kavun:module/math/pi), [`e`](kavun:module/math/e), [`phi`](kavun:module/math/phi), their square roots and the
logarithms [`ln2`](kavun:module/math/ln2), [`log2e`](kavun:module/math/log2e), [`ln10`](kavun:module/math/ln10), [`log10e`](kavun:module/math/log10e); the float bounds
[`max_float64`](kavun:module/math/max_float64), [`smallest_nonzero_float64`](kavun:module/math/smallest_nonzero_float64) and their 32-bit pair; and
the integer bounds, [`max_int64`](kavun:module/math/max_int64) / [`min_int64`](kavun:module/math/min_int64) down to the 8-bit pair.

**Failures.** A non-numeric argument raises kind `invalid_argument_type`; a wrong count, `wrong_num_arguments`. A
result outside the reals is the float's own error state, answered rather than raised (`math.acos(2)` → `NaN`,
`math.inf(1)` → `+Inf`): arithmetic on it raises, and `x.is_nan()` / `x.is_inf()` ask about it.

modules.name: os
modules.summary: The process and its environment: arguments, exit, environment variables, identity, the working directory.

doc.markdown: Files are [`fs`](kavun:module/fs)'s, other processes [`exec`](kavun:module/exec)'s, path text [`path`](kavun:module/path)'s.

doc.code:
os := import("os")

os.platform              // "linux", "darwin", …

doc.markdown:
**Failures.** Everything the world can refuse raises kind `io`, with the operation named in the message:
`(os.chdir) chdir /nope: no such file or directory`. A function whose success has no result answers `undefined`.

modules.name: path
modules.summary: Path TEXT with the host's separator — joining, splitting, cleaning.

doc.markdown: It never touches the file system (that is [`fs`](kavun:module/fs)), so it is pure and importable by default.

doc.code:
path := import("path")
path.join("a", "b", "../c")     // => "a/c"
path.split("/x/y.txt")          // => ["/x/", "y.txt"]

doc.markdown: Failures: `invalid_value` (`rel`, `match`), `invalid_argument_type` (a non-string), `wrong_num_arguments`.

doc.markdown: A root answers the separator itself.

functions.name: clean
functions.summary: Answer the shortest equivalent path.

doc.markdown: The result has no `.` or `..` elements and no doubled separators.

functions.name: split
functions.summary: Split `p` into directory and file, `dir` keeping its trailing separator so `dir + file == p`.

doc.markdown:
The module's one function is the constructor of the type it owns: `rand.generator(seed)` answers a
[`rand.generator`](kavun:type/rand.generator) whose draws are its own state. Pure — it reads nothing from the world,
so it is importable by default; entropy comes from `os.rand_generator()`, which answers the same type over
`crypto/rand`.

doc.code:
rand := import("rand")
g := rand.generator(1)
g.draw_int(1, 7)            // a die roll, [1, 7) — the same on every run with seed 1
g.draw_float()              // [0, 1)
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5].shuffle(g)  // a new array, shuffled with g's draws
os := import("os")          // os needs a grant
d := os.rand_generator()    // the same type, unpredictable

doc.markdown:
The generator's members (see [types/rand_generator.md](kavun:type/rand.generator)): `draw_int([lo,] hi)`,
`draw_float([lo,] hi)`, `draw_bytes(n)`, `draw_perm(n)`, `draw_norm()`, `draw_exp()`, `copy()`. Ranges are
half-open, like `range(lo, hi)`.

**Failures.** A bound that leaves no value (`g.draw_int(5, 5)`) or a bad count (`g.draw_bytes(0)`) raises `invalid_value`.

functions.name: generator
functions.summary: Answer a generator seeded with `seed`.

doc.markdown:
`seed` is an `int`.

The same seed gives the same sequence on every build: the source is PCG-DXSM (a specified algorithm) and every draw
is derived from its raw output by Kavun's own code. A reproducible run seeds from a literal; a seed from entropy is
`rand.generator(os.rand_generator().draw_int())`.

The seed is required: a pure module cannot pick one itself.

The module's one function is the constructor of the type it owns: `re.pattern(src)` compiles the expression once, and
the [`re.pattern`](kavun:type/re.pattern) answers `match`, `find`, `replace` and `split`. Pure: importable by
default.

doc.code:
re := import("re")
digits := re.pattern("[0-9]+")
digits.match("abc123")              // => true
digits.find("a1b22")                // => [[{"begin": 1, "end": 2, "text": "1"}]] — the first match, group 0 first
digits.find("a1b22", -1).len()      // => 2 — every match
digits.find("abc")                  // => [] — no match is an empty array, never undefined
digits.replace("a1b22", "#")        // => "a#b#"
re.pattern(",\\s*").split("a, b,c")  // => ["a", "b", "c"]

doc.markdown:
The pattern's members (see [types/re_pattern.md](kavun:type/re.pattern)):

- `p.match(s) -> bool`: Whether the expression matches anywhere in `s`.
- `p.find(s, count?) -> [match]`: The first match (or up to `count`; `-1` for all), each an array of frozen
`{text, begin, end}` group records, group 0 first; `[]` when nothing matches.
- `p.replace(s, repl) -> string`: Every match replaced; `$1` / `${name}` expand groups. A replacement that would
grow past the sequence ceiling raises `invalid_value`.
- `p.split(s, count?) -> [string]`: `s` cut at the matches.
- `p.string() -> string`: The source text (the pattern IS text); `format(p)` renders `re.pattern("…")`.

**Failures.** An invalid expression raises kind `invalid_value` — a bad pattern is a bad argument:
`(re.pattern) error parsing regexp: missing closing ): `(``.

functions.name: pattern
functions.summary: Compile the regular expression `src`; a malformed expression raises `invalid_value`.

doc.markdown:
`src` is a `string`.

The expression is compiled where `re.pattern(…)` runs — hoist a pattern used in a loop.
